# Multilevel Dyson Brownian motions via the superposition principle

**Authors:** Benjamin Budway and Mykhaylo Shkolnikov Address: ORFE Department, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ 08544. Email address: bb2584@princeton.edu Address: Department of Mathematical Sciences, Carnegie Mellon University, Pittsburgh, PA 15232. Email address: mshkolni@gmail.com

## Abstract

Multilevel Dyson Brownian motions (MDBMs) combine Dyson Brownian motions of different dimensions into a single process in a canonical way. This paper completes the theory of MDBMs for $\beta\geq 2$ . Specifically, we use the superposition principle of Figalli and Trevisan to construct the MDBMs for all $\beta>2$ in a unified manner. This also extends their stochastic differential equation representation, first discovered in [16], to all $\beta>2$ and proves the uniqueness of the MDBMs for all $\beta>2$ . Finally, we show that their limit as $\beta\downarrow 2$ is given by the $\beta=2$ MDBM of [28], commonly referred to as the Warren process.

## 1. Introduction

Let $N\geq 2$ and consider the following stochastic process in the space of $N\times N$ Hermitian matrices: As the diagonal entries, take independent real standard Brownian motions; for the entries above the diagonal, choose the real and the imaginary parts to be independent real standard Brownian motions multiplied by $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$ . Dyson has famously shown in [13] that the (real) ordered eigenvalues $X_{1}(t)\leq X_{2}(t)\leq\cdots\leq X_{N}(t)$ of such a process obey the stochastic differential equation (SDE)

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{d}X_{i}(t)=\theta\sum_{j\neq i}\frac{1}{X_{i}(t)-X_{j}(t)}\,\mathrm{d}t+\mathrm{d}B_{i}(t),\quad i=1,\,2,\,\ldots,\,N $$

started from $X_{1}(0)=X_{2}(0)=\cdots=X_{N}(0)=0$ , where $\theta=1$ and $B=(B_{i})_{i=1}^{N}$ is a vector of independent real standard Brownian motions. It turns out (see [9, Theorem 3.1]) that (1.1) admits a unique strong solution for all $\theta>0$ , called $\theta$ -Dyson Brownian motion, or $\theta$ -DBM for short. (When the value of $\theta$ is apparent from the context, we omit the dependence on $\theta$ and simply write DBM.)

Next, fix a $t>0$ and consider not only the eigenvalues $X_{1}(t)\leq X_{2}(t)\leq\cdots\leq X_{N}(t)$ of the full $N\times N$ Hermitian matrix, but also the eigenvalues $X^{k}_{1}(t)\leq X^{k}_{2}(t)\leq\cdots\leq X^{k}_{k}(t)$ of its top left $k\times k$ submatrices for $k=1,\,2,\,\ldots,\,N-1$ . By a well-known theorem of Cauchy, these eigenvalues interlace in the sense that $X_{i}^{k+1}(t)\leq X_{i}^{k}(t)\leq X_{i+1}^{k+1}(t)$ for all $1\leq i\leq k\leq N-1$ , and thus induce a probability distribution on the Gelfand-Tsetlin cone

$$ \mathcal{K}:=\mathcal{K}_{N}:=\big\{(x_{i}^{k})_{1\leq i\leq k\leq N}:\,x_{i}^{k+1}\leq x_{i}^{k}\leq x_{i+1}^{k+1}\text{ for all }1\leq i\leq k\leq N-1\big\}. $$

The resulting probability measure is referred to as the $\theta=1$ Hermite corners process of variance $t$ . It can be characterized by two properties: The density of the random vector $(X^{N}_{i}(t))_{i=1}^{N}:=(X_{i}(t))_{i=1}^{N}$ is proportional to

$$ \displaystyle\prod_{1\leq i<j\leq N}(x_{j}^{N}-x_{i}^{N})^{2\theta}\,\prod_{i=1}^{N}\,\exp\bigg(\!-\frac{(x_{i}^{N})^{2}}{2t}\bigg), $$

and the Markov transition density from $X^{k}(t):=(X_{i}^{k}(t))_{i=1}^{k}=x^{k}$ to $X^{k-1}(t)$ is given by

$$ \displaystyle\lambda^{k,\theta}(x^{k},x^{k-1}):=\frac{\Gamma(k\theta)}{\Gamma(\theta)^{k}}\prod_{1\leq i<j\leq k-1}(x_{j}^{k-1}-x_{i}^{k-1})\,\prod_{i=1}^{{k-1}}\prod_{j=1}^{k}|x_{j}^{k}-x_{i}^{k-1}|^{\theta-1}\,\prod_{1\leq i<j\leq k}(x_{j}^{k}-x_{i}^{k})^{1-2\theta}, $$

the so-called Dixon-Anderson density, for $k=2,\,3,\,\ldots,\,N$ . Beyond the case $\theta=1$ , the described probability measure on $\mathcal{K}$ has a random matrix intepretation also for $\theta=\frac{1}{2}$ and $\theta=2$ , yielding the joint distribution of the ordered eigenvalues of the full matrix and of its top left $k\times k$ submatrices for $k=1,\,2,\,\ldots,\,N-1$ in the (scaled) Gaussian Orthogonal Ensemble (GOE) and in the (scaled) Gaussian Symplectic Ensemble (GSE), respectively. For more details on these two random matrix ensembles, see, e.g., [21, Chapters 6, 7].

The above suggest the existence of a process $(X^{k,\theta}_{i})_{1\leq i\leq k\leq N}$ in $\mathcal{K}$ such that $(X^{k,\theta}_{i})_{i=1}^{k}$ is a $\theta$ -DBM for all $k=1,\,2,\,\ldots,\,N$ and that $(X^{k,\theta}_{i}(t))_{1\leq i\leq k\leq N}$ is the $\theta$ -Hermite corners process of variance $t$ for all $t>0$ . For $\theta=1$ , such a process $(X^{k,\theta}_{i})_{1\leq i\leq k\leq N}$ has been constructed by Warren in the seminal paper [28]. His process is an appropriate (obliquely) reflected Brownian motion (RBM) in $\mathcal{K}$ , which exhibits the two aforementioned properties when started from $0\in\mathcal{K}$ . It is worth mentioning that Warren’s process is different from the (non-Markovian) process given by the eigenvalues of the full matrix and its $k\times k$ top left submatrices for $k=1,\,2,\,\ldots,\,N-1$ in the Hermitian matrix-valued process described at the beginning of this introduction (see [1]). For $\theta>1$ , the authors of [16] obtain, via a discrete-space Markov chain approximation based on Jack polynomials, a process ( $Y^{mu}$ in their notation) featuring the two desired properties. For $\theta\geq 2$ , it is further shown in [16] that their process satisfies the SDE

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{d}X_{i}^{k,\theta}(t)=(\theta-1)\bigg(\sum_{j=1}^{k-1}\frac{1}{X_{i}^{k,\theta}(t)-X_{j}^{k-1,\theta}(t)}-\sum_{j\neq i}\frac{1}{X_{i}^{k,\theta}(t)-X_{j}^{k,\theta}(t)}\bigg)\,\mathrm{d}t+\mathrm{d}B_{i}^{k}(t),\;1\leq i\leq k\leq N, $$

where $(B^{k}_{i})_{1\leq i\leq k\leq N}$ is a vector of independent real standard Brownian motions. In [16, Theorem 4.1], the existence of a unique $\mathcal{K}$ -valued weak solution to (1.5) is proved for $\theta>1$ and for initial conditions in the interior of $\mathcal{K}$ and $0\in\mathcal{K}$ . However, due to difficulties associated with hitting the boundary of $\mathcal{K}$ , the authors of [16] identify $Y^{mu}$ with the solution to (1.5) only for $\theta\geq 2$ .

A natural family of initial distributions on $\mathcal{K}$ that contains the Dirac mass at $0\in\mathcal{K}$ consists of the so-called $\theta$ -Gibbs distributions. These are the distributions of the form

$$ \mu_{0}\times\Lambda^{N,\theta}:=\mu_{0}(\mathrm{d}x^{N})\,\Lambda^{N,\theta}(x^{N},\mathrm{d}(x^{k}_{i})_{1\leq i\leq k\leq N-1}):=\mu_{0}(\mathrm{d}x^{N})\,\prod_{k=0}^{N-2}\lambda^{N-k,\theta}(x^{N-k},x^{N-k-1})\,\mathrm{d}x^{N-k-1}. $$

Our first main result handles all $\theta>1$ and all $\theta$ -Gibbs initial distributions (even those assigning a positive mass to the boundary of $\mathcal{K}$ ), in particular bridging the gap in understanding for $\theta\in(1,2)$ .

#### Theorem 1.1.

Fix a $\theta>1$ and a probability measure $\mu_{0}$ on the Weyl chamber

$$ \mathcal{W}:=\mathcal{W}_{N}:=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{N}\!:x_{1}\leq x_{2}\leq\cdots\leq x_{N}\}, $$

and for $t>0$ let $\mu_{t}$ be the time $t$ distribution of a $\theta$ -DBM started from $\mu_{0}$ . Then, there exists a $\mathcal{K}$ -valued weak solution $X^{\theta}$ to the SDE (1.5) with the initial distribution $\mu_{0}\times\Lambda^{N,\theta}$ such that

- (a) $X^{k,\theta}:=(X_{i}^{k,\theta})_{i=1}^{k}$ is a $\theta$ -DBM for all $k=1,\,2,\,\ldots,\,N$ ,

- (b) and for all $t\geq 0$ , $X^{\theta}(t)$ has the distribution $\mu_{t}\times\Lambda^{N,\theta}$ .

Moreover, the $\mathcal{K}$ -valued weak solution satisfying (b) is unique in distribution and Markovian.

The main tool we rely on to prove Theorem 1.1 is the superposition principle of Trevisan [26]. Given an SDE, a superposition principle guarantees that a measure-valued solution $(\nu_{t})_{t\in[0,T]}$ of the associated Fokker-Planck equation can be lifted to a solution of the associated martingale problem with the fixed time distributions $(\nu_{t})_{t\in[0,T]}$ . The literature on superposition principles goes back to DiPerna and Lions who studied the deterministic case in [12] (see also [3]). Figalli [14] was then the first to extend the result to the stochastic case, for bounded drift and diffusion coefficients. His result was, in turn, extended by Trevisan in [26] to cover drift and diffusion coefficients integrable with respect to the given fixed time distributions. A further extension can be found in [8], where drift and diffusion coefficients are allowed to grow faster at infinity.

In the setting of Theorem 1.1, checking that $\mu_{t}\times\Lambda^{N,\theta}$ , $t\geq 0$ solve the correct Fokker-Planck equation requires inverse moment estimates for the spacings in the $\theta$ -DBM, as well as in the Dixon-Anderson process. We hope that the new estimates for the Dixon-Anderson density can be combined with inputs about other processes, such as the $\beta$ -Laguerre and the $\beta$ -Jacobi processes (see, e.g., [5]), to construct further multilevel processes akin to the ones in Theorem 1.1.

Given Theorem 1.1, it is natural to wonder whether the processes $\{X^{\theta}\}_{\theta>1}$ therein converge to the Warren process as $\theta\downarrow 1$ . Our second contribution is to answer this question in the affirmative, at least when the limiting initial distribution $\mu_{0}$ does not assign mass to the boundary $\partial\mathcal{W}$ of $\mathcal{W}$ .

#### Theorem 1.2.

For each $\theta>1$ , let $\mu_{0}^{\theta}$ be a probability measure on $\mathcal{W}$ . Assume that as $\theta\downarrow 1$ , the measures $\mu_{0}^{\theta}$ converge weakly to $\mu_{0}$ , a probability measure on $\mathcal{W}$ with $\mu_{0}(\partial\mathcal{W})=0$ . If $X^{\theta}$ is the weak solution to (1.5) with the initial distribution $\mu_{0}^{\theta}\times\Lambda^{N,\theta}$ described in Theorem 1.1, then as $\theta\downarrow 1$ , the processes $X^{\theta}$ converge in distribution to the Warren process $X^{1}$ with the initial distribution $\mu_{0}\times\Lambda^{N,1}$ .

#### Remark 1.3.

Theorem 1.2 along with our estimates for the Dixon-Anderson density (see Section 2) and standard martingale problem techniques render the family $\{X^{\theta}\}_{\theta\geq 1}$ weakly continuous in $\theta$ .

The Warren process $X^{1}$ is a weak solution to an SDE with reflection (SDER), whose definition we recall in Section 5. To identify a limit point of $\{X^{\theta}\}_{\theta>1}$ as $\theta\downarrow 1$ with $X^{1}$ , we use the submartingale problem formulation of SDERs due to Kang and Ramanan [17]. The concept of submartingale problems was originally introduced by Stroock and Varadhan for smooth domains in [25], which prompted a large body of work on the equivalence between SDERs and submartingale problems, see, e.g., [27], [29], [19], [20], [10]. To the best of our knowledge, [17] is the first work to establish the equivalence between SDERs and submartingale problems in enough generality to include $X^{1}$ .

Central to the construction of the Warren process in [28] is the fact that the semigroups of $\theta=1$ DBMs of different dimensions are intertwined through the Dixon-Anderson (conditional) density. Thus, the Warren process can be viewed as a coupling of $\theta=1$ DBMs of different dimensions that realizes their intertwining, an idea originally proposed by Diaconis and Fill in [11] for Markov chains. More generally, it has been proved in [23] that, for any $\theta>0$ , the semigroups of $\theta$ -DBMs of different dimensions are intertwined (while analogues of this statement for the $\beta$ -Laguerre and the $\beta$ -Jacobi ensembles can be found in [5]). In the same vein, then, the process $X^{\theta}$ of Theorem 1.1 can be regarded as a coupling that realizes the latter intertwining.

The rest of the paper is structured as follows. In Section 2, we present useful results for the Dixon-Anderson density, including the aforementioned inverse moment estimates for spacings. In Section 3, we recall the superposition principle of [26] and show that it applies to $(\mu_{t}\times\Lambda^{N,\theta})_{t\geq 0}$ of Theorem 1.1. In Section 4, we rely on the results of Section 3 in order to prove Theorem 1.1. In Section 5, we review the results on submartingale problems from [17] and combine them with Theorem 1.1 to prove Theorem 1.2. Throughout, we rely on various estimates for the $\theta$ -DBM, the statements and proofs of which are collected in Appendix A.

## 2. Preliminaries on the Dixon-Anderson density

We start by verifying that $\Lambda^{N,\theta}$ solves an appropriate partial differential equation (PDE) classically in the interior $\overset{\circ}{\mathcal{K}}$ of $\mathcal{K}$ . To this end, we define the differential operators

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{A}^{\theta}_{N}f=\sum_{i=1}^{N}c_{i}^{N,\theta}\,\partial_{x_{i}^{N}}f+\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\partial_{x_{i}^{N}x_{i}^{N}}f, \displaystyle\mathcal{A}_{N-1}^{\theta,*}f=-\sum_{i=1}^{N-1}\partial_{x_{i}^{N-1}}(c_{i}^{N-1,\theta}f)+\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{N-1}\partial_{x_{i}^{N-1}x_{i}^{N-1}}f, \displaystyle\mathcal{L}^{\theta,*}_{1,...,N-1}f=-\sum_{1\leq i\leq k\leq N-1}\partial_{x_{i}^{k}}(b_{i}^{k,\theta}f)+\frac{1}{2}\sum_{1\leq i\leq k\leq N-1}\partial_{x_{i}^{k}x_{i}^{k}}f, $$

where

$$ c_{i}^{N,\theta}(x):=\theta\sum_{j\neq i}\frac{1}{x^{N}_{i}-x^{N}_{j}}\quad\text{and}\quad b_{i}^{k,\theta}(x):=(\theta-1)\bigg(\sum_{j=1}^{k-1}\,\frac{1}{x_{i}^{k}-x_{j}^{k-1}}-\sum_{j\neq i}\,\frac{1}{x_{i}^{k}-x_{j}^{k}}\bigg). $$

#### Lemma 2.1.

For any $\theta>0$ , the following PDEs hold classically in $\overset{\circ}{\mathcal{K}}$ :

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{A}_{N-1}^{\theta,*}\lambda^{N,\theta}=\mathcal{A}^{\theta}_{N}\lambda^{N,\theta}, \displaystyle\mathcal{L}^{\theta,*}_{1,...,N-1}\Lambda^{N,\theta}=\mathcal{A}^{\theta}_{N}\Lambda^{N,\theta}. $$

Proof. We fix a $\theta>0$ and omit $\theta$ in the superscripts. The two PDEs can be stated equivalently as

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\partial_{x_{i}^{N}x_{i}^{N}}\lambda^{N}+\sum_{i=1}^{N}c_{i}^{N}\,\partial_{x_{i}^{N}}\lambda^{N}=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{j=1}^{N-1}\partial_{x_{j}^{N-1}x_{j}^{N-1}}\lambda^{N}-\sum_{j=1}^{N-1}\partial_{x_{j}^{N-1}}(c_{j}^{N-1}\lambda^{N}), \displaystyle\sum_{1\leq i\leq k\leq N-1}\partial_{x_{i}^{k}}(b_{i}^{k}\Lambda^{N})+\sum_{i=1}^{N}\partial_{x_{i}^{N}x_{i}^{N}}\Lambda^{N}+\sum_{i=1}^{N}c^{N}_{i}\,\partial_{x_{i}^{N}}\Lambda^{N}=\frac{1}{2}\Delta\Lambda^{N}. $$

We start with the proof of (2.7). Let $L_{i,j}:=(x_{i}^{N}-x_{j}^{N-1})^{-1}$ for $i=1,2,\ldots,N$ and $j=1,2,\ldots,N-1$ , $B_{i,n}:=(x_{i}^{N}-x_{n}^{N})^{-1}$ for $i=1,\,2,\,\ldots,\,N$ and $n=1,\,2,\,\ldots,\,N$ , $n\neq i$ , and $D_{j,m}:=(x_{j}^{N-1}-x_{m}^{N-1})^{-1}$ for $j=1,\,2,\,\ldots,\,N-1$ and $m=1,\,2,\,\ldots,\,N-1$ , $m\neq j$ . Then, we write the derivatives in (2.7) as

$$ \displaystyle c_{i}^{N}\,\partial_{x_{i}^{N}}\lambda^{N}=\lambda^{N}\,\bigg(\theta(\theta-1)\Big(\sum_{n\neq i}B_{i,n}\Big)\Big(\sum_{j=1}^{N-1}L_{i,j}\Big)+\theta(1-2\theta)\Big(\sum_{n\neq i}B_{i,n}\Big)^{2}\bigg), \displaystyle\partial_{x_{i}^{N}x_{i}^{N}}\lambda^{N}=\lambda^{N}\,\bigg((\theta\!-\!1)\sum_{j=1}^{N-1}L_{i,j}+(1\!-\!2\theta)\sum_{n\neq i}B_{i,n}\bigg)^{2}-\lambda^{N}\bigg((\theta\!-\!1)\sum_{j=1}^{N-1}L_{i,j}^{2}+(1\!-\!2\theta)\sum_{n\neq i}B_{i,n}^{2}\bigg), \displaystyle\partial_{x_{j}^{N-1}}(c_{j}^{N-1}\lambda^{N})=\lambda^{N}\,\bigg(\theta\Big(\sum_{m\neq j}D_{j,m}\Big)^{2}-\theta\sum_{m\neq j}D_{j,m}^{2}-\theta(\theta-1)\Big(\sum_{m\neq j}D_{j,m}\Big)\Big(\sum_{i=1}^{N}L_{i,j}\Big)\bigg), \displaystyle\partial_{x_{j}^{N-1}x_{j}^{N-1}}\lambda^{N}=\lambda^{N}\,\bigg(\sum_{m\neq j}D_{j,m}-(\theta-1)\sum_{i=1}^{N}L_{i,j}\bigg)^{2}-\lambda^{N}\,\bigg(\sum_{m\neq j}D_{j,m}^{2}+(\theta-1)\sum_{i=1}^{N}L_{i,j}^{2}\bigg). $$

Next, following the argument on [4, p. 254], we compute

$$ \sum_{i=1}^{N}\bigg(\Big(\sum_{n\neq i}B_{i,n}\Big)^{2}-\sum_{n\neq i}B_{i,n}^{2}\bigg)=\sum_{i\neq n\neq l\neq i}\frac{1}{x_{i}^{N}-x_{n}^{N}}\,\frac{1}{x_{i}^{N}-x_{l}^{N}}\qquad\qquad\qquad $$

$$ \qquad\;=\sum_{i\neq n\neq l\neq i}\frac{1}{x_{l}^{N}-x_{n}^{N}}\,\Big(\frac{1}{x_{i}^{N}-x_{l}^{N}}-\frac{1}{x_{i}^{N}-x_{n}^{N}}\Big)=-2\sum_{i\neq n\neq l\neq i}\frac{1}{x_{i}^{N}-x_{n}^{N}}\,\frac{1}{x_{i}^{N}-x_{l}^{N}}. $$

By comparing the second expression to the fourth one, we infer that

$$ \sum_{i=1}^{N}\bigg(\Big(\sum_{n\neq i}B_{i,n}\Big)^{2}-\sum_{n\neq i}B_{i,n}^{2}\bigg)=0. $$

The same argument shows that

$$ \sum_{j=1}^{N-1}\bigg(\Big(\sum_{m\neq j}D_{j,m}\Big)^{2}-\sum_{m\neq j}D_{j,m}^{2}\bigg)=0. $$

These allow us to reduce the two sides of (2.7) to

$$ \displaystyle\lambda^{N}\,\bigg(\frac{1}{2}(\theta-1)^{2}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\Big(\sum_{j=1}^{N-1}L_{i,j}\Big)^{2}-(\theta-1)^{2}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\Big(\sum_{j=1}^{N-1}L_{i,j}\Big)\Big(\sum_{n\neq i}B_{i,n}\Big)-\frac{1}{2}(\theta-1)\sum_{i=1}^{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N-1}L_{i,j}^{2}\bigg), \displaystyle\lambda^{N}\,\bigg(\frac{1}{2}(\theta-1)^{2}\sum_{j=1}^{N-1}\Big(\sum_{i=1}^{N}L_{i,j}\Big)^{2}+(\theta-1)^{2}\sum_{j=1}^{N-1}\Big(\sum_{m\neq j}D_{j,m}\Big)\Big(\sum_{i=1}^{N}L_{i,j}\Big)-\frac{1}{2}(\theta-1)\sum_{j=1}^{N-1}\sum_{i=1}^{N}L_{i,j}^{2}\bigg). $$

Now, we expand the squares and move the cross terms, simplifying (2.7) to

$$ \sum_{j=1}^{N-1}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\sum_{n\neq i}\Big(\frac{1}{2}L_{i,j}L_{n,j}+B_{i,n}L_{i,j}\Big)=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N-1}\sum_{m\neq j}\Big(\frac{1}{2}L_{i,j}L_{i,m}-D_{j,m}L_{i,j}\Big). $$

Thanks to $L_{i,j}L_{n,j}=B_{i,n}(L_{n,j}-L_{i,j})$ and $L_{i,j}L_{i,m}=D_{j,m}(L_{i,j}-L_{i,m})$ , the equation reduces to

$$ \sum_{i=1}^{N}\sum_{n\neq i}B_{i,n}\sum_{j=1}^{N-1}(L_{i,j}+L_{n,j})=-\sum_{j=1}^{N-1}\sum_{m\neq j}D_{j,m}\sum_{i=1}^{N}(L_{i,j}+L_{i,m}). $$

Since $B_{i,n}=-B_{n,i}$ and $D_{m,j}=-D_{j,m}$ , both sides are equal to $0$ , and (2.7) readily follows.

We prove (2.8) by induction over $N$ . Since $\Lambda^{2}=\lambda^{2}$ and $\mathcal{L}^{\theta,*}_{1}=\mathcal{A}_{1}^{\theta,*}$ , the $N=2$ case follows by equation (2.7). Now, assume equation (2.8) holds for some $N\geq 2$ . We start with the first term in (2.8) for $N+1$ . Using the identities $\partial_{x_{i}^{N}}\Lambda^{N}=\Lambda^{N}(b_{i}^{N}-c_{i}^{N})$ and $\Lambda^{N+1}=\Lambda^{N}\lambda^{N+1}$ we find that

$$ \begin{split}&\,\sum_{1\leq i\leq k\leq N}\partial_{x_{i}^{k}}(b_{i}^{k}\Lambda^{N}\lambda^{N+1})=\lambda^{N+1}\sum_{1\leq i\leq k\leq N-1}\partial_{x_{i}^{k}}(b_{i}^{k}\Lambda^{N})+\sum_{i=1}^{N}\partial_{x_{i}^{N}}(b_{i}^{N}\Lambda^{N}\lambda^{N+1})\\
&=\lambda^{N+1}\sum_{1\leq i\leq k\leq N-1}\partial_{x_{i}^{k}}(b_{i}^{k}\Lambda^{N})+\sum_{i=1}^{N}\partial_{x_{i}^{N}}(\lambda^{N+1}\partial_{x_{i}^{N}}\Lambda^{N})+\sum_{i=1}^{N}\partial_{x_{i}^{N}}(\lambda^{N+1}c_{i}^{N}\Lambda^{N})\\
&=\lambda^{N+1}\Big(\sum_{1\leq i\leq k\leq N-1}\partial_{x_{i}^{k}}(b_{i}^{k}\Lambda^{N})+\sum_{i=1}^{N}\partial_{x_{i}^{N}x_{i}^{N}}\Lambda^{N}+\sum_{i=1}^{N}c_{i}^{N}\partial_{x_{i}^{N}}\Lambda^{N}\Big)+\nabla_{x^{N}}\lambda^{N+1}\cdot\nabla_{x^{N}}\Lambda^{N}\\
&\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\quad\;\;\;+\Lambda^{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\partial_{x_{i}^{N}}(c_{i}^{N}\lambda^{N+1})\\
&=\frac{1}{2}\lambda^{N+1}\Delta\Lambda^{N}+\nabla_{x^{N}}\lambda^{N+1}\cdot\nabla_{x^{N}}\Lambda^{N}+\Lambda^{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\partial_{x_{i}^{N}}(c_{i}^{N}\lambda^{N+1})\\
&=\frac{1}{2}\Delta\Lambda^{N+1}+\Lambda^{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\partial_{x_{i}^{N}}(c_{i}^{N}\lambda^{N+1})-\frac{1}{2}\Lambda^{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N+1}\partial_{x_{i}^{N+1}x_{i}^{N+1}}\lambda^{N+1}-\frac{1}{2}\Lambda^{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\partial_{x_{j}^{N}x_{j}^{N}}\lambda^{N+1}.\end{split} $$

Adding the other two terms on the left-hand side of (2.8) for $N+1$ we obtain

$$ \begin{split}&\,\frac{1}{2}\Delta\Lambda^{N+1}+\Lambda^{N}\Big(\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{N+1}\partial_{x_{i}^{N+1}x_{i}^{N+1}}\lambda^{N+1}\!+\!\sum_{i=1}^{N+1}c_{i}^{N+1}\partial_{x_{i}^{N+1}}\lambda^{N+1}\!+\!\sum_{i=1}^{N}\partial_{x_{i}^{N}}(c_{i}^{N}\lambda^{N+1})\!-\!\frac{1}{2}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\partial_{x_{j}^{N}x_{j}^{N}}\lambda^{N+1}\Big)\\
&=\frac{1}{2}\Delta\Lambda^{N+1},\end{split} $$

where we have used equation (2.7) for $N+1$ . ∎

The following crucial lemma, of interest in its own right, allows to control the inverses of spacings between points on consecutive levels in terms of those on the same level.

#### Lemma 2.2.

For all $k\in{\mathbb{N}}$ and $x^{k+1}\in\mathcal{W}_{k+1}$ , let

$$ \mathcal{R}(x^{k+1}):=\{z\in\mathbb{R}^{k}:\,x^{k+1}_{i}\leq z_{i}\leq x^{k+1}_{i+1},\,i=1,\,2,\,\ldots,\,k\}. $$

Then, for all $0\leq\alpha,\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2}<\theta$ and $a,b\in\{1,\,2,\,\ldots,\,k\}$ , $a\neq b$ :

$$ \begin{split}&\,\int_{\mathcal{R}(x^{k+1})}(x_{a+1}^{k+1}-x_{a}^{k})^{-\alpha}\,\lambda^{k+1}(x^{k+1},x^{k})\,\mathrm{d}x^{k}\leq\frac{C_{1}(k,\alpha,\theta)}{\theta-\alpha}\,(x_{a+1}^{k+1}-x_{a}^{k+1})^{-\alpha},\\
&\,\int_{\mathcal{R}(x^{k+1})}(x_{a+1}^{k+1}-x_{a}^{k})^{-\alpha_{1}}\,(x_{b+1}^{k+1}-x_{b}^{k})^{-\alpha_{2}}\,\lambda^{k+1}(x^{k+1},x^{k})\,\mathrm{d}x^{k}\\
&\leq\frac{C_{2}(k,\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},\theta)}{(\theta-\alpha_{1})(\theta-\alpha_{2})}\,(x_{a+1}^{k+1}-x_{a}^{k+1})^{-\alpha_{1}}\,(x_{b+1}^{k+1}-x_{b}^{k+1})^{-\alpha_{2}},\end{split} $$

where $C_{1}(k,\alpha,\theta):=\frac{\Gamma(\theta-\alpha+1)\,\Gamma((k+1)\theta)}{\Gamma(\theta)\,\Gamma((k+1)\theta-\alpha)}$ , $C_{2}(k,\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},\theta):=\frac{\Gamma(\theta-\alpha_{1}+1)\,\Gamma(\theta-\alpha_{2}+1)\,\Gamma((k+1)\theta)}{\Gamma(\theta)^{2}\,\Gamma((k+1)\theta-\alpha_{1}-\alpha_{2})}$ .

Proof. We only prove the second inequality, as the first can then be recovered by setting $\alpha_{2}=0$ in the second. The Dixon-Anderson identity (cf. [15, Proposition 4.2.1]) states that for $s_{1},\,s_{2},\,\ldots,\,s_{k+1}>0$ :

$$ \int_{\mathcal{R}(x^{k+1})}\prod_{i=1}^{k}\prod_{j=1}^{k+1}|z_{i}-x^{k+1}_{j}|^{s_{j}-1}\prod_{1\leq i<n\leq k}(z_{n}-z_{i})\,\mathrm{d}z=\frac{\prod_{j=1}^{k+1}\Gamma(s_{j})}{\Gamma(\sum_{j=1}^{k+1}s_{j})}\prod_{1\leq j<m\leq k+1}(x^{k+1}_{m}-x^{k+1}_{j})^{s_{m}+s_{j}-1}. $$

Moreover, denoting by $\delta_{\cdot,\cdot}$ the Kronecker delta, we can write

$$ \begin{split}&\,\int_{\mathcal{R}(x^{k+1})}\!(x_{a+1}^{k+1}\!-\!x_{a}^{k})^{-\alpha_{1}}\,(x_{b+1}^{k+1}\!-\!x_{b}^{k})^{-\alpha_{2}}\,\lambda^{k+1}(x^{k+1},x^{k})\,\mathrm{d}x^{k}=\frac{\Gamma((k+1)\theta)}{\Gamma(\theta)^{k+1}}\prod_{1\leq j<m\leq k+1}\!(x_{m}^{k+1}\!-\!x_{j}^{k+1})^{1-2\theta}\\
&\cdot\!\int_{\mathcal{R}(x^{k+1})}\!\prod_{1\leq i<n\leq k}(x_{n}^{k}\!-\!x_{i}^{k})\prod_{i=1}^{{k}}\prod_{j=1}^{k+1}|x_{j}^{k+1}\!-\!x_{i}^{k}|^{\theta-1-\alpha_{1}\delta_{j,a+1}-\alpha_{2}\delta_{j,b+1}}\prod_{\overset{i=1}{i\neq a}}^{k}|x_{a+1}^{k+1}\!-\!x_{i}^{k}|^{\alpha_{1}}\prod_{\overset{i=1}{i\neq b}}^{k}|x_{b+1}^{k+1}\!-\!x_{i}^{k}|^{\alpha_{2}}\,\mathrm{d}x^{k}.\end{split} $$

Thanks to the interlacing inequalities, $0\leq x_{a+1}^{k+1}-x_{i}^{k}\leq x_{a+1}^{k+1}-x_{i}^{k+1}$ , $i=1,\,2,\,\ldots,\,a-1$ , and $0\leq x_{i}^{k}-x_{a+1}^{k+1}\leq x_{i+1}^{k+1}-x_{a+1}^{k+1}$ , $i=a+1,\,a+2,\,\ldots,\,k$ . The same inequalities hold also with $a$ replaced by $b$ . Therefore, the above can be upper bounded by

$$ \begin{split}&\frac{\Gamma((k+1)\theta)}{\Gamma(\theta)^{k+1}}\prod_{1\leq j<m\leq k+1}(x_{m}^{k+1}-x_{j}^{k+1})^{1-2\theta}\prod_{j=1,j\neq a,j\neq a+1}^{k+1}|x_{a+1}^{k+1}-x_{j}^{k+1}|^{\alpha_{1}}\prod_{j=1,j\neq b,j\neq b+1}^{k+1}|x_{b+1}^{k+1}-x_{j}^{k+1}|^{\alpha_{2}}\\
&\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\;\,\cdot\int_{\mathcal{R}(x^{k+1})}\prod_{1\leq i<n\leq k}(x_{n}^{k}-x_{i}^{k})\,\prod_{i=1}^{{k}}\prod_{j=1}^{k+1}|x_{j}^{k+1}-x_{i}^{k}|^{\theta-1-\alpha_{1}\delta_{j,a+1}-\alpha_{2}\delta_{j,b+1}}\,\mathrm{d}x^{k}\\
&=\frac{\Gamma((k+1)\theta)}{\Gamma(\theta)^{k+1}}\prod_{1\leq j<m\leq k+1}(x_{m}^{k+1}\!-\!x_{j}^{k+1})^{1-2\theta}\prod_{j=1,j\neq a,j\neq a+1}^{k+1}|x_{a+1}^{k+1}\!-\!x_{j}^{k+1}|^{\alpha_{1}}\prod_{j=1,j\neq b,j\neq b+1}^{k+1}|x_{b+1}^{k+1}\!-\!x_{j}^{k+1}|^{\alpha_{2}}\end{split} $$

$$ \begin{split}\qquad\quad\;\;\,\cdot\frac{\Gamma(\theta)^{k-1}\,\Gamma(\theta-\alpha_{1})\,\Gamma(\theta-\alpha_{2})}{\Gamma((k+1)\theta-\alpha_{1}-\alpha_{2})}\prod_{1\leq j<m\leq k+1}(x_{m}^{k+1}-x_{j}^{k+1})^{2\theta-\alpha_{1}(\delta_{j,a+1}+\delta_{m,a+1})-\alpha_{2}(\delta_{j,b+1}+\delta_{m,b+1})-1}\\
=\frac{\Gamma(\theta-\alpha_{1})\,\Gamma(\theta-\alpha_{2})\,\Gamma((k+1)\theta)}{\Gamma(\theta)^{2}\,\Gamma((k+1)\theta-\alpha_{1}-\alpha_{2})}\,(x_{a+1}^{k+1}-x_{a}^{k+1})^{-\alpha_{1}}\,(x_{b+1}^{k+1}-x_{b}^{k+1})^{-\alpha_{2}}.\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\;\end{split} $$

To get the promised constant, we use that $(\theta-\alpha_{i})\,\Gamma(\theta-\alpha_{i})=\Gamma(\theta-\alpha_{i}+1)$ , $i=1,2$ . ∎

The next lemma lets us decouple the interactions in $\Lambda^{N}$ near $\partial\mathcal{K}$ . For $k=1,\,2,\,\ldots,\,N$ and $1\leq a\leq b\leq k$ , it uses the notation $x^{k}_{a,...,b}$ for the vector $(x^{k}_{i})_{i=a}^{b}$ .

#### Lemma 2.3.

Fix any $\theta\geq 1$ and pick an $\varepsilon\in(0,1]$ . For $x^{k+1}\in\mathcal{W}_{k+1}$ such that $x_{i}^{k+1}+2\varepsilon\leq x_{i+1}^{k+1}$ , $i=1,\,2,\,\ldots,\,k$ , define

$$ \mathcal{R}_{\varepsilon}(x^{k+1})=\{x^{k}\in\mathcal{R}(x^{k+1}):\,x_{i}^{k+1}+2\varepsilon\leq x_{i}^{k}+\varepsilon\leq x_{i+1}^{k+1},\,i=1,\,2,\,\ldots,\,k\}. $$

Then, for all $x^{k}\in\mathcal{R}_{\varepsilon}(x^{k+1})$ satisfying $x_{a}^{k}+\varepsilon=x_{a+1}^{k+1}$ , we have that

$$ \lambda^{k+1}(x^{k+1},x^{k})\leq C\varepsilon^{\theta-1}(x_{a+1}^{k+1}-x_{a}^{k+1})^{-\theta}\,\lambda^{a}(x_{1,...,a}^{k+1},x_{1,...,a-1}^{k})\,\lambda^{k-a+1}(x_{a+1,...,k+1}^{k+1},x_{a+1,...,k}^{k}). $$

Here, $C$ depends on $\theta,k$ and $a$ but not on $\varepsilon$ , and $\lambda_{1}$ is understood to be identically equal to $1$ .

Proof. We start by noting that

$$ \prod_{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle i=1}}{{i\neq a}}}^{k}|x_{i}^{k}-x_{a}^{k}|=\prod_{i=1}^{a-1}(x_{a+1}^{k+1}-\varepsilon-x_{i}^{k})\,\prod_{i=a+1}^{k}(x_{i}^{k}-x_{a+1}^{k+1}+\varepsilon). $$

Since $x^{k}\in\mathcal{R}_{\varepsilon}(x^{k+1})$ , it holds $x_{i}^{k}-x_{a+1}^{k+1}+\varepsilon\leq 2(x_{i}^{k}-x_{a+1}^{k+1})$ for $i=a+1,\,a+2,\,\ldots,\,k$ . Therefore, by the same argument used to get the upper bound (2.10), the above is at most

$$ \displaystyle 2^{k-a}\prod_{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle i=1}}{{i\neq a}}}^{k}|x_{i}^{k}-x_{a+1}^{k+1}|\leq 2^{k-a}\prod_{j=1,j\neq a,j\neq a+1}^{k+1}|x_{j}^{k+1}-x_{a+1}^{k+1}|. $$

In addition, the requirement $x^{k}\in\mathcal{R}(x^{k+1})$ implies that

$$ \displaystyle\prod_{i=1}^{a-1}\prod_{n=a+1}^{k}(x_{n}^{k}-x_{i}^{k})\leq\prod_{j=1}^{a-1}\prod_{m=a+2}^{k+1}(x_{m}^{k+1}-x_{j}^{k+1}). $$

Putting (2.11) and (2.12) together, we infer that

$$ \begin{split}&\prod_{1\leq i<n\leq k}(x_{n}^{k}-x_{i}^{k})\leq 2^{k-a}\prod_{1\leq i<n\leq a-1}(x_{n}^{k}-x_{i}^{k})\,\prod_{a+1\leq i<n\leq k}(x_{n}^{k}-x_{i}^{k})\\
&\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\;\;\cdot\prod_{j=1}^{a-1}|x_{j}^{k+1}-x_{a+1}^{k+1}|\,\prod_{j=a+2}^{k+1}|x_{j}^{k+1}-x_{a+1}^{k+1}|\,\prod_{j=1}^{a-1}\prod_{m=a+2}^{k+1}(x_{m}^{k+1}-x_{j}^{k+1})\\
&\leq 2^{k-a}(x_{a+1}^{k+1}-x_{a}^{k+1})^{-1}\prod_{1\leq i<n\leq a-1}(x_{n}^{k}-x_{i}^{k})\,\prod_{a+1\leq i<n\leq k}(x_{n}^{k}-x_{i}^{k})\,\prod_{j=1}^{a}\prod_{m=a+1}^{k+1}(x_{m}^{k+1}-x_{j}^{k+1}),\end{split} $$

where we applied $|x_{j}^{k+1}-x_{a+1}^{k+1}|\leq x_{j}^{k+1}-x_{a}^{k+1}$ , $j=a+2,\,a+3,\,\ldots,\,k+1$ in the last step.

For the double product in (1.4), we follow the derivation of (2.11), and then employ $x^{k+1}\in\mathcal{W}_{k+1}$ :

$$ \prod_{j=1}^{k+1}|x_{a}^{k}-x_{j}^{k+1}|^{\theta-1}\leq\varepsilon^{\theta-1}2^{(\theta-1)(k-a)}\prod_{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle j=1}}{{j\neq a+1}}}^{k+1}|x_{a+1}^{k+1}-x_{j}^{k+1}|^{\theta-1}\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\;\; $$

$$ \displaystyle\leq \displaystyle\!\!\!\!\varepsilon^{\theta-1}2^{(\theta-1)(k-a)}\prod_{j=1}^{a}|x_{a+1}^{k+1}-x_{j}^{k+1}|^{\theta-1}\prod_{j=a+2}^{k+1}|x_{a}^{k+1}-x_{j}^{k+1}|^{\theta-1} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\!\!\!\!\varepsilon^{\theta-1}2^{(\theta-1)(k-a)}(x_{a+1}^{k+1}-x_{a}^{k+1})^{-\theta+1}\prod_{j=1}^{a}|x_{a+1}^{k+1}-x_{j}^{k+1}|^{\theta-1}\prod_{j=a+1}^{k+1}|x_{a}^{k+1}-x_{j}^{k+1}|^{\theta-1}. $$

Due to $x^{k}\in\mathcal{R}(x^{k+1})$ , we have for $i=1,\,2,\,\ldots,\,a-1$ :

$$ \prod_{j=1}^{k+1}|x_{j}^{k+1}-x_{i}^{k}|^{\theta-1}\leq\prod_{j=1}^{a}|x_{j}^{k+1}-x_{i}^{k}|^{\theta-1}\prod_{j=a+1}^{k+1}|x_{j}^{k+1}-x_{i}^{k+1}|^{\theta-1}. $$

Therefore, it holds

$$ \begin{split}\prod_{i=1}^{a-1}\prod_{j=1}^{k+1}|x_{j}^{k+1}-x_{i}^{k}|^{\theta-1}&\leq\prod_{i=1}^{a-1}\prod_{j=1}^{a}|x_{j}^{k+1}-x_{i}^{k}|^{\theta-1}\,\prod_{m=1}^{a-1}\prod_{j=a+1}^{k+1}|x_{j}^{k+1}-x_{m}^{k+1}|^{\theta-1}\\
&=\prod_{i=1}^{a-1}\prod_{j=1}^{a}|x_{j}^{k+1}\!-\!x_{i}^{k}|^{\theta-1}\,\prod_{m=1}^{a}\prod_{j=a+1}^{k+1}|x_{j}^{k+1}\!-\!x_{m}^{k+1}|^{\theta-1}\,\Big(\prod_{j=a+1}^{k+1}|x_{j}^{k+1}\!-\!x_{a}^{k+1}|^{\theta-1}\Big)^{-1}.\end{split} $$

A similar argument shows that

$$ \begin{split}\prod_{i=a+1}^{k}\prod_{j=1}^{k+1}|x_{j}^{k+1}-x_{i}^{k}|^{\theta-1}\leq\prod_{i=a+1}^{k}\prod_{j=a+1}^{k+1}|x_{j}^{k+1}-x_{i}^{k}|^{\theta-1}\prod_{m=a+2}^{k+1}\prod_{j=1}^{a}|x_{j}^{k+1}-x_{m}^{k+1}|^{\theta-1}\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\quad\\
=\prod_{i=a+1}^{k}\prod_{j=a+1}^{k+1}|x_{j}^{k+1}\!-\!x_{i}^{k}|^{\theta-1}\prod_{m=a+1}^{k+1}\prod_{j=1}^{a}|x_{j}^{k+1}\!-\!x_{m}^{k+1}|^{\theta-1}\Big(\prod_{j=1}^{a}|x_{j}^{k+1}\!-\!x_{a+1}^{k+1}|^{\theta-1}\Big)^{-1}.\end{split} $$

Putting the inequalities (2.14), (2.15) and (2.16) together we arrive at

$$ \begin{split}\prod_{i=1}^{k}\prod_{j=1}^{k+1}|x_{i}^{k}-x_{j}^{k+1}|^{\theta-1}=\prod_{j=1}^{k+1}|x_{a}^{k}-x_{j}^{k+1}|^{\theta-1}\prod_{i=1}^{a-1}\prod_{j=1}^{k+1}|x_{i}^{k}-x_{j}^{k+1}|^{\theta-1}\prod_{i=a+1}^{k}\prod_{j=1}^{k+1}|x_{i}^{k}-x_{j}^{k+1}|^{\theta-1}\\
\leq\varepsilon^{\theta-1}2^{(\theta-1)(k-a)}(x_{a+1}^{k+1}-x_{a}^{k+1})^{-\theta+1}\prod_{j=1}^{a}|x_{a+1}^{k+1}-x_{j}^{k+1}|^{\theta-1}\prod_{j=a+1}^{k+1}|x_{a}^{k+1}-x_{j}^{k+1}|^{\theta-1}\quad\\
\cdot\prod_{i=1}^{a-1}\prod_{j=1}^{a}|x_{j}^{k+1}-x_{i}^{k}|^{\theta-1}\prod_{m=1}^{a}\prod_{j=a+1}^{k+1}|x_{j}^{k+1}-x_{m}^{k+1}|^{\theta-1}\Big(\prod_{j=a+1}^{k+1}|x_{j}^{k+1}-x_{a}^{k+1}|^{\theta-1}\Big)^{-1}\;\;\,\\
\cdot\prod_{i=a+1}^{k}\prod_{j=a+1}^{k+1}|x_{j}^{k+1}-x_{i}^{k}|^{\theta-1}\prod_{m=a+1}^{k+1}\prod_{j=1}^{a}|x_{j}^{k+1}-x_{m}^{k+1}|^{\theta-1}\Big(\prod_{j=1}^{a}|x_{j}^{k+1}-x_{a+1}^{k+1}|^{\theta-1}\Big)^{-1}\\
=\varepsilon^{\theta-1}2^{(\theta-1)(k-a)}(x_{a+1}^{k+1}-x_{a}^{k+1})^{-\theta+1}\prod_{m=1}^{a}\prod_{j=a+1}^{k+1}|x_{j}^{k+1}-x_{m}^{k+1}|^{2\theta-2}\qquad\qquad\qquad\quad\;\;\;\\
\cdot\prod_{i=1}^{a-1}\prod_{j=1}^{a}|x_{j}^{k+1}-x_{i}^{k}|^{\theta-1}\prod_{i=a+1}^{k}\prod_{j=a+1}^{k+1}|x_{j}^{k+1}-x_{i}^{k}|^{\theta-1}.\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\quad\;\end{split} $$

Thanks to the identity

$$ \begin{split}\prod_{1\leq j<m\leq k+1}(x_{m}^{k+1}-x_{j}^{k+1})^{1-2\theta}=&\,\prod_{j=1}^{a}\prod_{m=a+1}^{k+1}|x_{m}^{k+1}-x_{j}^{k+1}|^{1-2\theta}\\
&\cdot\prod_{1\leq j<m\leq a}(x_{m}^{k+1}-x_{j}^{k+1})^{1-2\theta}\prod_{a+1\leq j<m\leq k+1}(x_{m}^{k+1}-x_{j}^{k+1})^{1-2\theta},\end{split} $$

it remains to combine (2.13), (2.17) and (2.18) in order to obtain the lemma. ∎

Finally, we recall the intertwining between $\theta$ -DBMs of different dimensions established in [23, Theorem 1.1, Remark 1.2].

#### Proposition 2.4.

Fix any $\theta>0$ . For $k\in{\mathbb{N}}$ , let $(P_{t}^{k})_{t\geq 0}$ be the transition semigroup of a $\theta$ -DBM of dimension $k$ , and let $L^{k+1}$ be the transition operator associated with $\lambda^{k+1}$ . Then,

$$ \Big(\prod_{r=k+1}^{N}L^{r}\Big)\,P^{k}_{t}=P_{t}^{N}\,\Big(\prod_{r=k+1}^{N}L^{r}\Big),\quad t\geq 0,\quad N\geq k\geq 1, $$

where both sides are understood as transition operators taking bounded measurable functions on $\mathcal{W}_{k}$ to bounded measurable functions on $\mathcal{W}_{N}$ .

## 3. Superposition principle

Take any $\theta>1$ , $N\in{\mathbb{N}}$ and $T>0$ . Let $\mu_{0}$ be a probability measure on $\mathcal{W}_{N}$ and let $(\mu_{t})_{t\in[0,T]}$ be the fixed time distributions of a $\theta$ -DBM started from $\mu_{0}$ . The main goal of this section is to prove that the curve $(\nu_{t})_{t\in[0,T]}:=(\mu_{t}\times\Lambda^{N,\theta})_{t\in[0,T]}$ of probability measures can be lifted to a solution of the martingale problem associated with the SDE (1.5), an instance of the “superposition principle”. We start by giving a brief summary of the superposition principle in the form of [26].

### 3.1. Summary of the superposition principle

A curve $(\nu_{t})_{t\in[0,T]}$ of probability measures on ${\mathbb{R}}^{d}$ is called Borel if $t\rightarrow\nu_{t}(A)$ is Borel measurable for every Borel $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d}$ . Given any measurable $b\!:[0,T]\times{\mathbb{R}}^{d}\to{\mathbb{R}}^{d}$ and symmetric positive semidefinite $a\!:[0,T]\times{\mathbb{R}}^{d}\to{\mathbb{R}}^{d\times d}$ , let

$$ \mathcal{L}:=\mathcal{L}_{a,b,t}:=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i,j=1}^{d}a_{ij}(t,\cdot)\,\partial_{x_{i}x_{j}}+\sum_{i=1}^{d}b_{i}(t,\cdot)\,\partial_{x_{i}}. $$

Write $\mathcal{A}_{c}$ for the space of $C^{1,2}$ functions compactly supported in $(0,T)\times\mathbb{R}^{d}$ , and $\mathcal{A}$ for the space of bounded, continuous functions on $[0,T]\times\mathbb{R}^{d}$ with bounded first derivative in $t$ and bounded first and second derivatives in $x$ on $(0,T)\times\mathbb{R}^{d}$ .

#### Definition 3.1.

A Borel $(\nu_{t})_{t\in[0,T]}$ is a weak solution of the Fokker-Planck equation $\partial_{t}\nu_{t}=\mathcal{L}^{*}\nu_{t}$ if

$$ \displaystyle\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}|a(t,x)|+|b(t,x)|\,\nu_{t}(\mathrm{d}x)\,\mathrm{d}t<\infty, $$

and for every $f\in\mathcal{A}_{c}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\partial_{t}f(t,x)+\mathcal{L}f(t,x)\,\nu_{t}(\mathrm{d}x)\,\mathrm{d}t=0. $$

#### Definition 3.2.

Let $\eta$ be a probability measure on $C([0,T],\mathbb{R}^{d})$ , and let $e_{t}$ , $t\in[0,T]$ denote the coordinate mappings. Then, $\eta$ is said to solve the martingale problem associated with $a$ and $b$ if

$$ \int_{C([0,T],\mathbb{R}^{d})}\int_{0}^{T}|a|(t,\cdot)\circ e_{t}+|b|(t,\cdot)\circ e_{t}\,\mathrm{d}t\,\mathrm{d}\eta<\infty, $$

and for each $f\in\mathcal{A}$ , the following process is a martingale under $\eta$ with respect to the natural filtration:

$$ f(t,\cdot)\circ e_{t}-\int_{0}^{t}\partial_{s}f(s,\cdot)\circ e_{s}+\mathcal{L}f(s,\cdot)\circ e_{s}\,\mathrm{d}s,\quad t\in[0,T]. $$

The following “superposition principle” can be found in [26, Theorem 2.5].

#### Proposition 3.3.

If a Borel weakly continuous $(\nu_{t})_{t\in[0,T]}$ is a weak solution of the Fokker-Planck equation $\partial_{t}\nu_{t}=\mathcal{L}^{*}\nu_{t}$ , then there exists a solution $\eta$ of the corresponding martingale problem such that $\eta\circ e_{t}^{-1}=\nu_{t}$ , $t\in[0,T]$ .

### 3.2. Superposition principle in our context

In this subsection, we verify (3.2) and (3.3) for $(\nu_{t})_{t\in[0,T]}:=(\mu_{t}\times\Lambda^{N,\theta})_{t\in[0,T]}$ and $\mathcal{L}:=\mathcal{L}_{1,...,N}:=\frac{1}{2}\Delta+b\cdot\nabla$ , where

$$ b_{i}^{k}(x):=\sum_{j=1}^{k-1}\frac{\theta-1}{x_{i}^{k}-x_{j}^{k-1}}-\sum_{j\neq i}\frac{\theta-1}{x_{i}^{k}-x_{j}^{k}},\quad 1\leq i\leq k\leq N. $$

The proof is broken into six steps. In Step 1, we show (3.2). In Steps 2, 3 and 4, we establish (3.3) for a restricted class of initial distributions $\mu_{0}$ and of test functions $f$ . In Steps 5 and 6, we extend (3.3) to all $f\in\mathcal{A}_{c}$ and to all probability measures $\mu_{0}$ on $\mathcal{W}_{N}$ , respectively.

Step 1. In order to show (3.2), it suffices to check

$$ \int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathcal{K}}|b_{i}^{k}(x)|\,\nu_{t}(\mathrm{d}x)\,\mathrm{d}t<\infty $$

for all $1\leq i\leq k\leq N$ , $k\geq 2$ . With $C$ being a finite positive constant that changes from line to line,

$$ |b_{i}^{k}(x)|=\bigg|\sum_{j=1}^{k-1}\frac{\theta-1}{x_{i}^{k}-x_{j}^{k-1}}-\sum_{j\neq i}\frac{\theta-1}{x_{i}^{k}-x_{j}^{k}}\bigg|\leq C\bigg(\frac{1}{x_{i}^{k}-x_{i-1}^{k-1}}+\frac{1}{x_{i}^{k-1}-x_{i}^{k}}\bigg). $$

For $x^{N}\in\mathcal{W}_{N}$ and $m=1,\,2,\,\ldots,\,N-1$ , we define

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{K}(x^{N})=\big\{(x_{i}^{k})_{1\leq i\leq k\leq N-1}:\,x_{i}^{k+1}\leq x_{i}^{k}\leq x_{i+1}^{k+1},\,1\leq i\leq k\leq N-1\big\}, \displaystyle\mathcal{K}^{m}(x^{N})=\big\{(x_{i}^{k})_{1\leq i\leq k,\,m\leq k\leq N-1}:\,x_{i}^{k+1}\leq x_{i}^{k}\leq x_{i+1}^{k+1},\,1\leq i\leq k,\,m\leq k\leq N-1\big\}. $$

Then, by Lemma 2.2,

$$ \displaystyle\int_{\mathcal{K}}|b_{i}^{k}(x)|\,\nu_{t}(\mathrm{d}x)=\int_{\mathcal{W}_{N}}\int_{\mathcal{K}(x^{N})}|b_{i}^{k}(x)|\,\Lambda^{N,\theta}(x)\,\mathrm{d}x^{1}\,\ldots\,\mathrm{d}x^{N-1}\,\mu_{t}(\mathrm{d}x^{N}) \displaystyle\qquad\;\;\;\leq C\int_{\mathcal{W}_{N}}\int_{\mathcal{K}^{k}(x^{N})}\bigg(\frac{1}{x_{i}^{k}-x_{i-1}^{k}}+\frac{1}{x_{i+1}^{k}-x_{i}^{k}}\bigg)\,\prod_{m=k+1}^{N}\lambda^{m,\theta}(x^{m},x^{m-1})\,\mathrm{d}x^{k}\,\ldots\,\mathrm{d}x^{N-1}\,\mu_{t}(\mathrm{d}x^{N}) \displaystyle\qquad\;\;\;=C\,\mathbb{E}\bigg[\frac{1}{X_{i}^{k}(t)-X_{i-1}^{k}(t)}+\frac{1}{X_{i+1}^{k}(t)-X_{i}^{k}(t)}\bigg], $$

where $X^{k}(t)$ is obtained by sampling first a $\theta$ -DBM $X^{N}$ with the initial distribution $\mu_{0}$ , and then $X^{k}(t)$ according to the Dixon-Anderson density. By Lemma 2.4, a copy of $X^{k}(t)$ can be obtained by sampling first $X^{N}(0)$ according to $\mu_{0}$ , then $X^{k}(0)$ according to the Dixon-Anderson density, and finally $X^{k}(t)$ according to the transition operator of the $\theta$ -DBM. Thus, the integral from $0$ to $T$ of the upper bound (3.5) is finite by Lemma A.3(a).

Step 2. Now, assume additionally that $\mu_{0}(\mathrm{d}x^{N})=p_{0}(x^{N})\,\mathrm{d}x^{N}$ for some $p_{0}\in L^{1}(\mathcal{W}_{N})$ satisfying

$$ \mathrm{supp}(p_{0})\subset\,\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\circ}}{{\mathcal{W}}}_{N}\text{compactly and }\int_{\mathcal{W}_{N}}|\log p_{0}(x^{N})|\,p_{0}(x^{N})\,\mathrm{d}x^{N}<\infty. $$

Then, by Lemma A.5, $\mu_{t}$ admits a density $p_{t}\in W^{1}_{1}(\mathcal{W}_{N})$ for $t\in(0,T]$ . Also, let $f\in C^{1,2}_{c}((0,T)\times\mathcal{K})$ be such that for some $\varepsilon_{0}>0$ , $f(t,x)=0$ if $\mathrm{dist}(x^{N},\partial{\mathcal{W}_{N}})<\varepsilon_{0}$ . Further, define the operators

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{1,...,N-1}=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{1\leq i\leq k\leq N-1}\partial_{x_{i}^{k}x_{i}^{k}}+\sum_{1\leq i\leq k\leq N-1}b_{i}^{k}\,\partial_{x_{i}^{k}}, \displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{N}=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\partial_{x_{i}^{N}x_{i}^{N}}+\sum_{i=1}^{N}b_{i}^{N}\,\partial_{x_{i}^{N}}. $$

In Steps 2, 3 and 4, we study respectively

$$ \displaystyle\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathcal{K}}\partial_{t}f(t,x)\,p_{t}(x^{N})\,\Lambda^{N,\theta}(x)\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}t, \displaystyle\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathcal{K}}(\mathcal{L}_{N}f)(t,x)\,p_{t}(x^{N})\,\Lambda^{N,\theta}(x)\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}t, \displaystyle\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathcal{K}}(\mathcal{L}_{1,...,N-1}f)(t,x)\,p_{t}(x^{N})\,\Lambda^{N,\theta}(x)\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}t. $$

While dealing with (3.8) and (3.9), we drop the superscript of $N$ in $b^{N}$ and $c^{N}$ . The function

$$ h(t,x^{N}):=\int_{\mathcal{K}(x^{N})}f(t,x)\,\Lambda^{N,\theta}(x)\,\mathrm{d}x^{1}\,\ldots\,\mathrm{d}x^{N-1} $$

belongs to $C_{c}^{1,1}((0,T)\times\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\circ}}{{\mathcal{W}}}_{N})$ by Lemma 2.2, the identity $\nabla_{x^{N}}\Lambda^{N,\theta}=(b-c)\Lambda^{N,\theta}$ , and the boundedness of $\partial_{t}f$ and $\nabla_{x^{N}}f$ . Therefore, by Lemma A.6,

$$ \begin{split}\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathcal{K}}\partial_{t}f(t,x)\,p_{t}(x^{N})\,\Lambda^{N,\theta}(x)\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}t&=\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathcal{W}_{N}}\partial_{t}h(t,x^{N})\,p_{t}(x^{N})\,\mathrm{d}x^{N}\,\mathrm{d}t\\
&=\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathcal{W}_{N}}-c\cdot(\nabla_{x^{N}}h)\,p_{t}+\frac{1}{2}\nabla_{x^{N}}h\cdot\nabla_{x^{N}}p_{t}\,\mathrm{d}x^{N}\,\mathrm{d}t.\end{split} $$

Finally, $|\nabla_{x^{N}}\Lambda^{N,\theta}|$ is integrable over $\mathcal{K}(x^{N})$ for any $x^{N}\in\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\circ}}{{\mathcal{W}}}_{N}$ by Lemma 2.2. This, the boundedness of $f$ and $|\nabla_{x^{N}}f|$ , and $\Lambda^{N,\theta}(x^{N},\cdot)\equiv 0$ on the codimension one part of $\partial\mathcal{K}(x^{N})$ yield

$$ \nabla_{x^{N}}\int_{\mathcal{K}(x^{N})}f(t,x)\,\Lambda^{N,\theta}(x)\,\mathrm{d}x^{1}\,\ldots\,\mathrm{d}x^{N-1}=\int_{\mathcal{K}(x^{N})}\nabla_{x^{N}}(f\Lambda^{N,\theta})\,\mathrm{d}x^{1}\,\ldots\,\mathrm{d}x^{N-1}. $$

All in all, the term in (3.8) equals to

$$ \displaystyle\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathcal{K}}-c\cdot\nabla_{x^{N}}(f\Lambda^{N,\theta})\,p_{t}+\frac{1}{2}\nabla_{x^{N}}(f\Lambda^{N,\theta})\cdot\nabla_{x^{N}}p_{t}\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}t. $$

Step 3. We turn to (3.9). Since $\nabla_{x^{N}}\Lambda^{N,\theta}=(b-c)\Lambda^{N,\theta}$ , we have that

$$ \int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathcal{K}}(\mathcal{L}_{N}f)\,p_{t}\,\Lambda^{N,\theta}\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}t=\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathcal{K}}\big(c\cdot\nabla_{x^{N}}f+\frac{1}{2}\Delta_{x^{N}}f\big)\,p_{t}\,\Lambda^{N,\theta}\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}t+\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathcal{K}}(\nabla_{x^{N}}f\cdot\nabla_{x^{N}}\Lambda^{N,\theta})\,p_{t}\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}t. $$

We seek to integrate by parts. To this end, for $\varepsilon>0$ , we let

$$ \mathcal{K}_{\varepsilon}:=\{x\in\mathcal{K}:\,x_{i}^{N}+2\varepsilon\leq x_{i}^{N-1}+\varepsilon\leq x_{i+1}^{N},\,i=1,\,2,\,\ldots,\,N-1\}, $$

and let $\mathcal{K}^{m}_{\varepsilon}$ be the $(x_{i}^{k})_{1\leq i\leq k,\,m\leq k\leq N}$ projection of $\mathcal{K}_{\varepsilon}$ . Since $\Delta_{x^{N}}f$ is bounded,

$$ \lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow 0}\,\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathcal{K}\setminus\mathcal{K}_{\varepsilon}}|\Delta_{x^{N}}f|\,p_{t}\,\Lambda^{N,\theta}\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}t=0. $$

Write $\kappa(x)=(\kappa_{i}^{k}(x))_{1\leq i\leq k\leq N}$ for the outward normal to $\partial\mathcal{K}_{\varepsilon}$ at $x\in\partial\mathcal{K}_{\varepsilon}$ , and set

$$ \displaystyle D_{i,+,\varepsilon}=\{x\in\partial\mathcal{K}_{\varepsilon}:\,x_{i-1}^{N-1}+\varepsilon=x_{i}^{N}\},\quad i=2,\,3,\,\ldots,\,N, \displaystyle D_{i,-,\varepsilon}=\{x\in\partial\mathcal{K}_{\varepsilon}:\,x_{i}^{N-1}-\varepsilon=x_{i}^{N}\},\quad i=1,\,2,\,\ldots,\,N-1. $$

Then, $\kappa_{i}^{N}\neq 0$ only on $D_{i,+,\varepsilon}$ and $D_{i,-,\varepsilon}$ . Integrating by parts, we find that

$$ \begin{split}\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathcal{K}_{\varepsilon}}\partial_{x_{i}^{N}x_{i}^{N}}f\,p_{t}\,\Lambda^{N,\theta}\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}t=&\,-\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathcal{K}_{\varepsilon}}\partial_{x_{i}^{N}}f\,\partial_{x_{i}^{N}}(p_{t}\Lambda^{N,\theta})\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}t\\
&\,+\int_{0}^{T}\int_{D_{i,+,\varepsilon}}\partial_{x_{i}^{N}}f\,p_{t}\,\Lambda^{N,\theta}\,\kappa_{i}^{N}\,\mathrm{d}S\,\mathrm{d}t+\int_{0}^{T}\int_{D_{i,-,\varepsilon}}\partial_{x_{i}^{N}}f\,p_{t}\,\Lambda^{N,\theta}\,\kappa_{i}^{N}\,\mathrm{d}S\,\mathrm{d}t.\end{split} $$

We only consider the $D_{i,+,\varepsilon}$ term, as the $D_{i,-,\varepsilon}$ term can be studied similarly. Let $0<t_{1}<t_{2}<T$ be such that $f(t,x)=0$ unless $t\in[t_{1},t_{2}]$ . Estimating $\partial_{x_{i}^{N}}f$ and $\kappa_{i}^{N}$ by constants, integrating out $x^{1},\,\ldots,\,x^{N-2}$ , using Lemma 2.3, and integrating out $x^{N-1}_{1},\,\ldots,\,x^{N-1}_{i-2},\,x^{N-1}_{i},\,\ldots,\,x^{N-1}_{N-1}$ we infer that

$$ \begin{split}\bigg|\int_{0}^{T}\int_{D_{i,+,\varepsilon}}\partial_{x_{i}^{N}}f\,p_{t}\,\Lambda^{N,\theta}\,\kappa_{i}^{N}\,\mathrm{d}S\,\mathrm{d}t\bigg|&\leq C\varepsilon^{\theta-1}\int_{t_{1}}^{t_{2}}\int_{\mathcal{W}_{N}}(x_{i}^{N}-x_{i-1}^{N})^{-\theta}\,p_{t}(x^{N})\,\mathrm{d}x^{N}\,\mathrm{d}t\\
&=C\varepsilon^{\theta-1}\int_{t_{1}}^{t_{2}}\mathbb{E}\big[(X_{i}^{N}(t)-X_{i-1}^{N}(t))^{-\theta}\big]\,\mathrm{d}t,\end{split} $$

where $X^{N}$ is a $\theta$ -DBM with the initial distribution $\mu_{0}$ . The latter integral is finite by Lemma A.3(c), and so the overall expression goes to $0$ with $\varepsilon$ .

Finally, we argue that $\partial_{x_{i}^{N}}f\,\partial_{x_{i}^{N}}(p_{t}\Lambda^{N,\theta})$ is integrable over $(0,T)\times\mathcal{K}$ . Bounding $\partial_{x_{i}^{N}}f$ by a constant and applying Lemma 2.2 we see that, on the one hand,

$$ \begin{split}&\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathcal{K}}|\partial_{x_{i}^{N}}f\,\partial_{x_{i}^{N}}\Lambda^{N,\theta}|\,p_{t}\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}t\leq C\int_{t_{1}}^{t_{2}}\int_{\mathcal{W}_{N}}\int_{\mathcal{R}(x^{N})}|b_{i}^{N}-c_{i}^{N}|\,\lambda^{N,\theta}\,p_{t}\,\mathrm{d}x^{N-1}\,\mathrm{d}x^{N}\,\mathrm{d}t\\
&\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\quad\leq C\int_{t_{1}}^{t_{2}}\int_{\mathcal{W}_{N}}\int_{\mathcal{R}(x^{N})}\big((x_{i}^{N}-x_{i-1}^{N-1})^{-1}+(x_{i}^{N-1}-x_{i}^{N})^{-1}\big)\,\lambda^{N,\theta}\,p_{t}\,\mathrm{d}x^{N-1}\,\mathrm{d}x^{N}\,\mathrm{d}t\\
&\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\quad\leq C\int_{t_{1}}^{t_{2}}\int_{\mathcal{W}_{N}}\big((x_{i}^{N}-x_{i-1}^{N})^{-1}+(x_{i+1}^{N}-x_{i}^{N})^{-1}\big)\,p_{t}\,\mathrm{d}x^{N}\,\mathrm{d}t\\
&\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\quad=C\int_{t_{1}}^{t_{2}}\mathbb{E}\big[(X_{i}^{N}(t)-X_{i-1}^{N}(t))^{-1}+(X_{i+1}^{N}(t)-X_{i}^{N}(t))^{-1}\big]\,\mathrm{d}t,\end{split} $$

where the last integral is finite by Lemma A.3(c). On the other hand, Hölder’s inequality implies

$$ \begin{split}\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathcal{K}}|\partial_{x_{i}^{N}}f\,\partial_{x_{i}^{N}}p_{t}|\,\Lambda^{N,\theta}\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}t&\leq C\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathcal{W}_{N}}|\partial_{x_{i}^{N}}p_{t}|\,\mathrm{d}x^{N}\,\mathrm{d}t\\
&\leq C\bigg(\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathcal{W}_{N}}p_{t}\,\mathrm{d}x^{N}\,\mathrm{d}t\bigg)^{1/2}\,\bigg(\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathcal{W}_{N}}\frac{|\nabla_{x^{N}}p_{t}|^{2}}{p_{t}}\,\mathrm{d}x^{N}\,\mathrm{d}t\bigg)^{1/2},\end{split} $$

where the last double integral is finite by Lemma A.5. All in all, we have shown that

$$ \int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathcal{K}}(\Delta_{x^{N}}f)\,p_{t}\,\Lambda^{N,\theta}\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}t=-\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathcal{K}}\nabla_{x^{N}}f\cdot\nabla_{x^{N}}(p_{t}\Lambda^{N,\theta})\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}t. $$

Thus, the term in (3.9) equals to

$$ \displaystyle\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathcal{K}}(c\cdot\nabla_{x^{N}}f)\,p_{t}\,\Lambda^{N,\theta}-\frac{1}{2}\nabla_{x^{N}}f\cdot\nabla_{x^{N}}(p_{t}\Lambda^{N,\theta})+(\nabla_{x^{N}}f\cdot\nabla_{x^{N}}\Lambda^{N,\theta})\,p_{t}\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}t. $$

Step 4. In this (most involved) step, we deal with the term in (3.10). By Lemma 2.1,

$$ \int_{\mathcal{K}_{\varepsilon}}\sum_{1\leq i\leq k\leq N-1}\Big(-fp_{t}\,\partial_{x_{i}^{k}}(b_{i}^{k}\Lambda^{N,\theta})+\frac{1}{2}fp_{t}\,\partial_{x_{i}^{k}x^{k}_{i}}\Lambda^{N,\theta}\Big)\,\mathrm{d}x=\int_{\mathcal{K}_{\varepsilon}}fp_{t}\,c^{N}\cdot\nabla_{x^{N}}\Lambda^{N,\theta}+\frac{1}{2}fp_{t}\,\Delta_{x^{N}}\Lambda^{N,\theta}\,\mathrm{d}x. $$

Now, we integrate by parts on both sides. Recalling that $p_{t}$ is a function of $x^{N}$ only, we find that

$$ \begin{split}&\,\int_{\mathcal{K}_{\varepsilon}}\sum_{1\leq i\leq k\leq N-1}\Big(b_{i}^{k}\Lambda^{N,\theta}\,p_{t}\,\partial_{x_{i}^{k}}f+\frac{1}{2}\Lambda^{N,\theta}\,p_{t}\,\partial_{x_{i}^{k}x^{k}_{i}}f\Big)\,\mathrm{d}x\\
&=\int_{\mathcal{K}_{\varepsilon}}fp_{t}\,c^{N}\cdot\nabla_{x^{N}}\Lambda^{N,\theta}-\frac{1}{2}\nabla_{x^{N}}(fp_{t})\cdot\nabla_{x^{N}}\Lambda^{N,\theta}\,\mathrm{d}x+R_{1}(t)+R_{2}(t),\end{split} $$

where the boundary terms are given by

$$ \begin{split}&R_{1}(t)=\int_{\partial\mathcal{K}_{\varepsilon}}fp_{t}\,\Big(\sum_{1\leq i\leq k\leq N-1}\Big(b_{i}^{k}\Lambda^{N,\theta}-\frac{1}{2}\partial_{x_{i}^{k}}\Lambda^{N,\theta}\Big)\,\kappa_{i}^{k}+\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\partial_{x_{i}^{N}}\Lambda^{N,\theta}\,\kappa_{i}^{N}\Big)\,\mathrm{d}S,\\
&R_{2}(t)=\frac{1}{2}\int_{\partial\mathcal{K}_{\varepsilon}}\sum_{1\leq i\leq k\leq N-1}p_{t}\Lambda^{N,\theta}\,\partial_{x_{i}^{k}}f\,\kappa_{i}^{k}\,\mathrm{d}S,\end{split} $$

and $\kappa_{i}^{k}$ is the $(k,i)$ component of the outward normal to $\partial\mathcal{K}_{\varepsilon}$ .

We first aim to show that the integrals of $|R_{2}(t)|$ and of $|R_{1}(t)|$ with respect to $t$ tend to $0$ with $\varepsilon$ . Note that $\partial\mathcal{K}_{\varepsilon}\subset\bigcup_{1\leq i\leq k\leq N-1}(D_{k,i,+,\varepsilon}\cup D_{k,i,-,\varepsilon})$ , where

$$ D_{k,i,+,\varepsilon}:=\{x\in\partial\mathcal{K}_{\varepsilon}:\,x_{i}^{k}+\varepsilon=x_{i+1}^{k+1}\}\quad\text{and}\quad D_{k,i,-,\varepsilon}:=\{x\in\partial\mathcal{K}_{\varepsilon}:\,x_{i}^{k}-\varepsilon=x_{i}^{k+1}\}. $$

Also, for $m=1,\,2,\,\ldots,\,N$ , let $\mathcal{K}^{m}$ be the $(x_{i}^{k})_{1\leq i\leq k\leq N,\,k\geq m}$ projection of $\mathcal{K}$ . Bounding $\partial_{x_{j}^{m}}f$ and $\kappa^{m}_{j}$ by constants, integrating out $x^{1},\,\ldots,\,x^{k-1}$ , using Lemma 2.3, and finally integrating out $x^{k}_{1},\,\ldots,\,x^{k}_{i-1},\,x^{k}_{i+1},\,\ldots,x^{k}_{k}$ we see that

$$ \begin{split}&\,\int_{D_{k,i,+,\varepsilon}}\sum_{1\leq j\leq m\leq N-1}|p_{t}\Lambda^{N,\theta}\,\partial_{x_{j}^{m}}f\,\kappa_{j}^{m}|\,\mathrm{d}S\\
&\leq C\,\mathbf{1}_{[t_{1},t_{2}]}(t)\,\varepsilon^{\theta-1}\int_{\mathcal{K}^{k+1}}(x_{i+1}^{k+1}-x_{i}^{k+1})^{-\theta}\prod_{m=k+2}^{N}\lambda^{m,\theta}(x^{m},x^{m-1})\,p_{t}(x^{N})\,\mathrm{d}x^{k+1}\,\ldots\,\mathrm{d}x^{N}\\
&=C\,\mathbf{1}_{[t_{1},t_{2}]}(t)\,\varepsilon^{\theta-1}\,\mathbb{E}\big[(X_{i+1}^{k+1}(t)-X_{i}^{k+1}(t))^{-\theta}\big],\end{split} $$

where $X^{k+1}$ is a $\theta$ -DBM with the initial density

$$ \int_{\mathcal{K}^{k+2}}\mu_{0}(\mathrm{d}x^{N})\,\prod_{m=k+2}^{N}\lambda^{m,\theta}(x^{m},x^{m-1})\,\mathrm{d}x^{k+2}\,\ldots\,\mathrm{d}x^{N-1}, $$

and we have made use of Lemma 2.4. A similar argument shows that

$$ \int_{D_{k,i,-,\varepsilon}}\sum_{1\leq j\leq m\leq N-1}|p_{t}\Lambda^{N,\theta}\,\partial_{x_{j}^{m}}f\,\kappa_{j}^{m}|\,\mathrm{d}S\leq C\,\mathbf{1}_{[t_{1},t_{2}]}(t)\,\varepsilon^{\theta-1}\,\mathbb{E}\big[(X_{i}^{k+1}(t)-X_{i-1}^{k+1}(t))^{-\theta}\big]. $$

In conclusion,

$$ \int_{0}^{T}|R_{2}(t)|\,\mathrm{d}t\leq C\varepsilon^{\theta-1}\int_{t_{1}}^{t_{2}}\sum_{1\leq i\leq k\leq N-1}\mathbb{E}\big[(X_{i+1}^{k+1}(t)-X_{i}^{k+1}(t))^{-\theta}\big]\,\mathrm{d}t, $$

which goes to $0$ with $\varepsilon$ thanks to Lemma A.3(c).

We turn to the more complicated $R_{1}(t)$ . Consider $D_{k,i,+,\varepsilon}$ for fixed $1\leq i\leq k\leq N-2$ . On $D_{k,i,+,\varepsilon}$ , it holds $\kappa_{i}^{k}\equiv-\kappa_{i+1}^{k+1}$ , and $\kappa^{m}_{j}\equiv 0$ for all other $(m,j)$ . Therefore,

$$ \begin{split}&\,\bigg|\int_{D_{k,i,+,\varepsilon}}fp_{t}\,\Big(\sum_{1\leq j\leq m\leq N-1}\Big(b_{j}^{m}\Lambda^{N,\theta}-\frac{1}{2}\partial_{x_{j}^{m}}\Lambda^{N,\theta}\Big)\,\kappa_{j}^{m}+\frac{1}{2}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\partial_{x_{j}^{N}}\Lambda^{N,\theta}\,\kappa_{j}^{N}\Big)\,\mathrm{d}S\bigg|\\
&\leq C\,\mathbf{1}_{[t_{1},t_{2}]}(t)\int_{D_{k,i,+,\varepsilon}}p_{t}\,\Big|b_{i}^{k}\Lambda^{N,\theta}-\frac{1}{2}\partial_{x_{i}^{k}}\Lambda^{N,\theta}-b_{i+1}^{k+1}\Lambda^{N,\theta}+\frac{1}{2}\partial_{x_{i+1}^{k+1}}\Lambda^{N,\theta}\Big|\,\mathrm{d}S.\end{split} $$

Recalling the definition of $b^{k}_{i}$ in (2.4), as well as

$$ \partial_{x_{i}^{k}}\Lambda^{N,\theta}(x)=\Lambda^{N,\theta}(x)\,\bigg((\theta-1)\sum_{j=1}^{k-1}\frac{1}{x_{i}^{k}-x_{j}^{k-1}}+2(1-\theta)\sum_{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle j=1}}{{j\neq i}}}^{k}\frac{1}{x_{i}^{k}-x_{j}^{k}}+(\theta-1)\sum_{j=1}^{k+1}\frac{1}{x_{i}^{k}-x_{j}^{k+1}}\bigg), $$

we note that the terms involving $(x_{i+1}^{k+1}-x_{i}^{k})^{-1}$ in $-\frac{1}{2}\partial_{x_{i}^{k}}\Lambda^{N,\theta}$ , $-b_{i+1}^{k+1}\Lambda^{N,\theta}$ , and $\frac{1}{2}\partial_{x_{i+1}^{k+1}}\Lambda^{N,\theta}$ cancel out exactly! Thus, we have the estimate (with obvious adjustments if $i=1$ or $i=k$ ):

$$ \begin{split}&\,\mathbf{1}_{[t_{1},t_{2}]}(t)\int_{D_{k,i,+,\varepsilon}}p_{t}\,\Big|b_{i}^{k}\Lambda^{N,\theta}-\frac{1}{2}\partial_{x_{i}^{k}}\Lambda^{N,\theta}-b_{i+1}^{k+1}\Lambda^{N,\theta}+\frac{1}{2}\partial_{x_{i+1}^{k+1}}\Lambda^{N,\theta}\Big|\,\mathrm{d}S\\
&\leq C\,\mathbf{1}_{[t_{1},t_{2}]}(t)\int_{D_{k,i,+,\varepsilon}}p_{t}(x^{N})\,\Lambda^{N,\theta}(x)\bigg(\frac{1}{x_{i}^{k-1}-x_{i}^{k}}+\frac{1}{x_{i}^{k}-x_{i-1}^{k-1}}+\frac{1}{x_{i}^{k}-x_{i}^{k+1}}\\
&\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\;\;\;+\frac{1}{x_{i+1}^{k}-x_{i+1}^{k+1}}+\frac{1}{x_{i+1}^{k+1}-x_{i+1}^{k+2}}+\frac{1}{x_{i+2}^{k+2}-x_{i+1}^{k+1}}\bigg)\,\mathrm{d}S.\end{split} $$

We deal with the terms in (3.15) one by one in the order of their appearance. Letting $D^{m}_{k,i,+,\varepsilon}$ be the respective $(x^{n}_{j})_{1\leq j\leq n\leq N,\,n\geq m}$ projections of $D_{k,i,+,\varepsilon}$ for $m=1,\,2,\,\ldots,\,k$ , integrating out $x^{1},\,\ldots,\,x^{k-2}$ , and using Lemma 2.2 we obtain

$$ \begin{split}&\,\mathbf{1}_{[t_{1},t_{2}]}(t)\int_{D_{k,i,+,\varepsilon}^{k-1}}\frac{p_{t}(x^{N})}{x_{i}^{k-1}-x_{i}^{k}}\,\prod_{m=k}^{N}\lambda^{m,\theta}(x^{m},x^{m-1})\,\mathrm{d}S\\
&\leq C\,\mathbf{1}_{[t_{1},t_{2}]}(t)\int_{D_{k,i,+,\varepsilon}^{k}}\frac{p_{t}(x^{N})}{x_{i+1}^{k}-x_{i}^{k}}\,\prod_{m=k+1}^{N}\lambda^{m,\theta}(x^{m},x^{m-1})\,\mathrm{d}S\\
&\leq C\,\mathbf{1}_{[t_{1},t_{2}]}(t)\int_{D_{k,i,+,\varepsilon}^{k}}\frac{p_{t}(x^{N})}{x_{i+1}^{k}-x_{i+1}^{k+1}}\,\prod_{m=k+1}^{N}\lambda^{m,\theta}(x^{m},x^{m-1})\,\mathrm{d}S.\end{split} $$

Note that the following argument also takes care of the fourth term in (3.15). Applying Lemma 2.3 as in the proof of inequality (3.14), and then Lemma 2.2 again, we find the upper bound

$$ \begin{split}&\,C\,\mathbf{1}_{[t_{1},t_{2}]}(t)\,\varepsilon^{\theta-1}\int_{\mathcal{K}^{k+1}}p_{t}(x^{N})\,(x_{i+1}^{k+1}-x_{i}^{k+1})^{-\theta}(x_{i+2}^{k+1}-x_{i+1}^{k+1})^{-1}\prod_{m=k+2}^{N}\lambda^{m,\theta}(x^{m},x^{m-1})\,\mathrm{d}x^{k+1}\,\ldots\,\mathrm{d}x^{N}\\
&=C\,\mathbf{1}_{[t_{1},t_{2}]}(t)\,\varepsilon^{\theta-1}\,\mathbb{E}\big[(X_{i+1}^{k+1}(t)-X_{i}^{k+1}(t))^{-\theta}(X_{i+2}^{k+1}(t)-X_{i+1}^{k+1}(t))^{-1}\big].\end{split} $$

We have used Lemma 2.4 to claim the latter equality. Integrating in $t$ and employing Lemma A.3(c), we see that the contribution from the first term in (3.15) goes to $0$ with $\varepsilon$ . The second term in (3.15) can be upper bounded in the same manner by

$$ C\,\mathbf{1}_{[t_{1},t_{2}]}(t)\,\varepsilon^{\theta-1}\,\mathbb{E}\big[(X_{i+1}^{k+1}(t)-X_{i}^{k+1}(t))^{-\theta}(X_{i}^{k+1}(t)-X_{i-1}^{k+1}(t))^{-1}\big]. $$

For the third term in (3.15), we apply $(x_{i}^{k}-x_{i}^{k+1})^{-1}\leq 2(x_{i+1}^{k+1}-x_{i}^{k+1})^{-1}$ , $x\in D_{k,i,+,\varepsilon}$ , and then Lemma 2.3 as in the proof of inequality (3.14) to obtain the upper bound

$$ C\,\mathbf{1}_{[t_{1},t_{2}]}(t)\,\varepsilon^{\theta-1}\,\int_{\mathcal{K}^{k+1}}p_{t}(x^{N})\,(x_{i+1}^{k+1}-x_{i}^{k+1})^{-\theta-1}\prod_{m=k+2}^{N}\lambda^{m,\theta}(x^{m},x^{m-1})\,\mathrm{d}x^{k+1}\,\ldots\,\mathrm{d}x^{N}. $$

In view of Lemma 2.4, this equals to

$$ C\,\mathbf{1}_{[t_{1},t_{2}]}(t)\,\varepsilon^{\theta-1}\,\mathbb{E}\big[(X_{i+1}^{k+1}(t)-X_{i}^{k+1}(t))^{-\theta-1}\big]. $$

Integrating in $t$ and recalling Lemma A.3(c) we see that the contribution from the third term in (3.15) goes to $0$ with $\varepsilon$ .

For the fifth term in (3.15), we rely on Lemma 2.3 to get

$$ \begin{split}&\,\mathbf{1}_{[t_{1},t_{2}]}(t)\int_{D_{k,i,+,\varepsilon}}p_{t}(x^{N})\,\Lambda^{N,\theta}(x)\,(x_{i+1}^{k+1}-x_{i+1}^{k+2})^{-1}\,\mathrm{d}S\\
&\leq C\mathbf{1}_{[t_{1},t_{2}]}(t)\varepsilon^{\theta-1}\int_{\mathcal{K}_{\varepsilon}^{k+1}}p_{t}(x^{N})(x_{i+1}^{k+1}\!-\!x_{i}^{k+1})^{-\theta}(x_{i+1}^{k+1}\!-\!x_{i+1}^{k+2})^{-1}\prod_{m=k+2}^{N}\lambda^{m,\theta}(x^{m},x^{m-1})\,\mathrm{d}x^{k+1}\,\ldots\,\mathrm{d}x^{N}\\
&\leq C\mathbf{1}_{[t_{1},t_{2}]}(t)\varepsilon^{\theta-1}\int_{\mathcal{K}_{\varepsilon}^{k+1}}p_{t}(x^{N})(x_{i+1}^{k+2}\!-\!x_{i}^{k+1})^{-\theta}(x_{i+1}^{k+1}\!-\!x_{i+1}^{k+2})^{-1}\prod_{m=k+2}^{N}\lambda^{m,\theta}(x^{m},x^{m-1})\,\mathrm{d}x^{k+1}\,\ldots\,\mathrm{d}x^{N}.\end{split} $$

Now, let $\alpha\in(0,\theta-1)$ and estimate the latter expression from above by

$$ C\mathbf{1}_{[t_{1},t_{2}]}(t)\varepsilon^{\theta-1-\alpha}\int_{\mathcal{K}_{\varepsilon}^{k+1}}\!p_{t}(x^{N})(x_{i+1}^{k+2}-x_{i}^{k+1})^{-\theta+\alpha}(x_{i+1}^{k+1}-x_{i+1}^{k+2})^{-1}\prod_{m=k+2}^{N}\!\lambda^{m,\theta}(x^{m},x^{m-1})\,\mathrm{d}x^{k+1}\ldots\,\mathrm{d}x^{N}. $$

Thanks to Lemmas 2.2 and 2.4, this can be bounded further by

$$ C\,\mathbf{1}_{[t_{1},t_{2}]}(t)\,\varepsilon^{\theta-1-\alpha}\,\mathbb{E}\big[(X_{i+1}^{k+2}(t)-X_{i}^{k+2}(t))^{-\theta+\alpha}(X_{i+2}^{k+2}(t)-X_{i+1}^{k+2}(t))^{-1}\big]. $$

Integrating in $t$ and using Lemma A.3(c) we infer that the contribution from the fifth term in (3.15) goes to $0$ with $\varepsilon$ . A similar argument also takes care of the sixth term in (3.15). Moreover, the $D_{k,i,-,\varepsilon}$ terms can be dealt with analogously.

In the case $k=N-1$ , we note that

$$ \begin{split}&\,\bigg|\sum_{i=1}^{N-1}\int_{D_{N-1,i,+,\varepsilon}}fp_{t}\,\Big(\sum_{1\leq j\leq m\leq N-1}\Big(b_{j}^{m}\Lambda^{N,\theta}-\frac{1}{2}\partial_{x_{j}^{m}}\Lambda^{N,\theta}\Big)\,\kappa_{j}^{m}+\frac{1}{2}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\partial_{x_{j}^{N}}\Lambda^{N,\theta}\,\kappa_{j}^{N}\Big)\,\mathrm{d}S\bigg|\\
&\leq C\,\mathbf{1}_{[t_{1},t_{2}]}(t)\sum_{i=1}^{N-1}\int_{D_{N-1,i,+,\varepsilon}}p_{t}\,\Big|\Big(b_{i}^{N-1}\Lambda^{N,\theta}-\frac{1}{2}\partial_{x_{i}^{N-1}}\Lambda^{N,\theta}\Big)\,\kappa_{i}^{N-1}+\frac{1}{2}\partial_{x_{i+1}^{N}}\Lambda^{N,\theta}\,\kappa_{i+1}^{N}\Big|\,\mathrm{d}S\\
&\leq C\,\mathbf{1}_{[t_{1},t_{2}]}(t)\sum_{i=1}^{N-1}\int_{D_{N-1,i,+,\varepsilon}}p_{t}\,\Big|b_{i}^{N-1}\Lambda^{N,\theta}-\frac{1}{2}\partial_{x_{i}^{N-1}}\Lambda^{N,\theta}-\frac{1}{2}\partial_{x_{i+1}^{N}}\Lambda^{N,\theta}\Big|\,\mathrm{d}S.\end{split} $$

Again, the crucial singularity $(x_{i+1}^{N}-x_{i}^{N-1})^{-1}$ cancels out on $D_{N-1,i,+\varepsilon}$ , resulting in the upper bound

$$ C\,\mathbf{1}_{[t_{1},t_{2}]}(t)\int_{D_{N-1,i,+,\varepsilon}}p_{t}(x^{N})\,\Lambda^{N,\theta}(x)\bigg(\frac{1}{x_{i}^{N-1}\!-\!x_{i-1}^{N-2}}+\frac{1}{x_{i}^{N-2}\!-\!x_{i}^{N-1}}+\frac{1}{x_{i}^{N-1}\!-\!x_{i}^{N}}+\frac{1}{x_{i+1}^{N-1}\!-\!x_{i+1}^{N}}\bigg)\,\mathrm{d}S. $$

It remains to proceed as with the first four terms in (3.15).

We proved that the contributions of the remainder terms in (3.13) go to $0$ with $\varepsilon$ . In order to get

$$ \begin{split}&\,\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathcal{K}}\sum_{1\leq i\leq k\leq N-1}\Big(b_{i}^{k}\,\Lambda^{N,\theta}p_{t}\,\partial_{x_{i}^{k}}f+\frac{1}{2}\Lambda^{N,\theta}\,p_{t}\,\partial_{x_{i}^{k}x_{i}^{k}}f\Big)\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}t\\
&=\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathcal{K}}fp_{t}\,c^{N}\cdot\nabla_{x^{N}}\Lambda^{N,\theta}-\frac{1}{2}\nabla_{x^{N}}(fp_{t})\cdot\nabla_{x^{N}}\Lambda^{N,\theta}\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}t,\end{split} $$

it remains to check the integrability on the right-hand side. (Note that the integrability on the left-hand side follows from the boundedness of $\partial_{x_{i}^{k}}f$ , $\partial_{x_{i}^{k}x_{i}^{k}}f$ , and Step 1.) For the first term, $\nabla_{x^{N}}\Lambda^{N,\theta}=(b^{N}-c^{N})\Lambda^{N,\theta}$ , Lemma 2.2, and the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality yield

$$ \begin{split}\int_{\mathcal{K}}|f|\,|c^{N}\cdot\nabla_{x^{N}}\Lambda^{N,\theta}|\,p_{t}\,\mathrm{d}x&\leq C\,\mathbf{1}_{[t_{1},t_{2}]}(t)\sum_{i=1}^{N}\bigg(\int_{\mathcal{K}}p_{t}\,|c_{i}^{N}|\,|b_{i}^{N}|\,\Lambda^{N,\theta}\,\mathrm{d}x+\int_{\mathcal{K}}p_{t}\,|c_{i}^{N}|^{2}\,\Lambda^{N,\theta}\,\mathrm{d}x\bigg)\\
&\leq C\,\mathbf{1}_{[t_{1},t_{2}]}(t)\sum_{i=1}^{N}\,\int_{\mathcal{W}_{N}}p_{t}(x^{N})\,\bigg(\frac{1}{(x_{i}^{N}-x_{i-1}^{N})^{2}}+\frac{1}{(x_{i+1}^{N}-x_{i}^{N})^{2}}\bigg)\,\mathrm{d}x^{N},\end{split} $$

which is integrable in $t$ by Lemma A.3(c).

For the second term on the right-hand side of (3.16), we use Lemmas 2.2 and A.3(c) to find

$$ \sum_{i=1}^{N}\,\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathcal{K}}p_{t}\,|\partial_{x_{i}^{N}}f\,\partial_{x_{i}^{N}}\Lambda^{N,\theta}|\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}t\leq C\sum_{i=1}^{N}\,\int_{t_{1}}^{t_{2}}\int_{\mathcal{W}_{N}}p_{t}(x^{N})\,\bigg(\frac{1}{x_{i}^{N}-x_{i-1}^{N}}+\frac{1}{x_{i+1}^{N}-x_{i}^{N}}\bigg)\,\mathrm{d}x^{N}\,\mathrm{d}t<\infty. $$

Finally, by $\nabla_{x^{N}}\Lambda^{N,\theta}=(b^{N}-c^{N})\Lambda^{N,\theta}$ and Lemma 2.2,

$$ \begin{split}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\,\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathcal{K}}|f|\,|\partial_{x_{i}^{N}}p_{t}\,\partial_{x_{i}^{N}}\Lambda^{N,\theta}|\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}t&\leq C\sum_{i=1}^{N}\,\int_{t_{1}}^{t_{2}}\int_{\mathcal{K}}|\partial_{x_{i}^{N}}p_{t}|\,|b_{i}^{N}|\,\Lambda^{N,\theta}+|\partial_{x_{i}^{N}}p_{t}|\,|c_{i}^{N}|\,\Lambda^{N,\theta}\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}t\\
&\leq C\sum_{i=1}^{N}\,\int_{t_{1}}^{t_{2}}\int_{\mathcal{W}_{N}}|\partial_{x_{i}^{N}}p_{t}(x^{N})|\,\bigg(\frac{1}{x_{i}^{N}-x_{i-1}^{N}}+\frac{1}{x_{i+1}^{N}-x_{i}^{N}}\bigg)\,\mathrm{d}x^{N}\,\mathrm{d}t.\end{split} $$

In view of the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, the latter expression is at most

$$ C\sum_{i=1}^{N}\bigg(\int_{t_{1}}^{t_{2}}\int_{\mathcal{W}_{N}}p_{t}(x^{N})\bigg(\frac{1}{(x_{i}^{N}-x_{i-1}^{N})^{2}}+\frac{1}{(x_{i+1}^{N}-x_{i}^{N})^{2}}\bigg)\,\mathrm{d}x^{N}\,\mathrm{d}t\bigg)^{1/2}\,\bigg(\int_{t_{1}}^{t_{2}}\int_{\mathcal{W}_{N}}\frac{|\nabla p_{t}|^{2}}{p_{t}}\,\mathrm{d}x^{N}\,\mathrm{d}t\bigg)^{1/2}, $$

which is finite by Lemmas A.3(c) and A.5. This finishes the proof of equation (3.16). Lastly, we combine (3.11), (3.12) and (3.16) to arrive at

$$ \begin{split}&\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathcal{K}}(\partial_{t}f+\mathcal{L}_{1,...,N}f)\,p_{t}\,\Lambda^{N,\theta}\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}t=\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathcal{K}}-c^{N}\cdot\nabla_{x^{N}}(f\Lambda^{N,\theta})\,p_{t}+\frac{1}{2}\nabla_{x^{N}}(f\Lambda^{N,\theta})\cdot\nabla_{x^{N}}p_{t}\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}t\\
&\qquad\qquad\qquad\quad\;\;+\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathcal{K}}(c^{N}\cdot\nabla_{x^{N}}f)\,p_{t}\,\Lambda^{N,\theta}-\frac{1}{2}\nabla_{x^{N}}f\cdot\nabla_{x^{N}}(p_{t}\Lambda^{N,\theta})+(\nabla_{x^{N}}f\cdot\nabla_{x^{N}}\Lambda^{N,\theta})\,p_{t}\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}t\\
&\qquad\qquad\qquad\quad\;\;+\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathcal{K}}fp_{t}\,c^{N}\cdot\nabla_{x^{N}}\Lambda^{N,\theta}-\frac{1}{2}\nabla_{x^{N}}(fp_{t})\cdot\nabla_{x^{N}}\Lambda^{N,\theta}\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}t=0.\end{split} $$

Step 5. Next, we remove the assumption that for some $\varepsilon_{0}>0$ , $f(t,x)=0$ if $\mathrm{dist}(x^{N},\partial\mathcal{W}_{N})<\varepsilon_{0}$ . Given an $\varepsilon>0$ , let $\zeta_{\varepsilon}\!:[0,\infty)\rightarrow[0,1]$ be a $C^{2}([0,\infty))$ -function such that $\zeta_{\varepsilon}(y)=0$ for $y\leq\varepsilon$ , $\zeta_{\varepsilon}(y)=1$ for $y\geq 2\varepsilon$ , $|\zeta^{\prime}_{\varepsilon}|\leq C\varepsilon^{-1}\,\mathbf{1}_{\{y\geq\varepsilon\}}$ , and $|\zeta^{\prime\prime}_{\varepsilon}|\leq C\varepsilon^{-2}\,\mathbf{1}_{\{y\geq\varepsilon\}}$ . Take $\phi_{\varepsilon}(x)=\prod_{i=1}^{N-1}\zeta_{\varepsilon}(x_{i+1}^{N}-x_{i}^{N})$ .

#### Lemma 3.4.

For every $f\in\mathcal{A}_{c}$ , there exists a constant $C_{f,\theta}<\infty$ (independent of $\mu_{0}$ ) so that

$$ \bigg|\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathcal{K}}\partial_{t}(f-f\phi_{\varepsilon})+\mathcal{L}_{1,...,N}(f-f\phi_{\varepsilon})\,\mathrm{d}\nu_{t}\,\mathrm{d}t\bigg|\leq C_{f,\theta}\,\varepsilon^{\theta-1},\quad\varepsilon\in(0,1). $$

Proof of Lemma 3.4. Let $X^{N}$ be a $\theta$ -DBM with the initial distribution $\mu_{0}$ , and let $Z^{N}$ be a $\theta$ -DBM started from $0\in\mathcal{W}_{N}$ . Write $\mathrm{dist}$ for the notion of distance on $\mathbb{R}^{N}$ induced by the infinity norm. Then, $\mathrm{dist}(x^{N},\partial\mathcal{W}_{N})\leq\min_{1\leq i\leq N-1}|x_{i+1}^{N}-x_{i}^{N}|\leq 2\,\mathrm{dist}(x^{N},\partial\mathcal{W}_{N})$ . By Lemmas A.1(b) and A.3(b),

$$ \begin{split}\mu_{t}\big(\{x^{N}\in\mathcal{W}_{N}:\,\mathrm{dist}(x^{N},\partial\mathcal{W}_{N})\leq 2\varepsilon\}\big)&\leq\sum_{i=1}^{N-1}\mathbb{P}(|X_{i+1}^{N}(t)-X_{i}^{N}(t)|\leq 4\varepsilon)\\
&\leq 4^{2\theta}\varepsilon^{2\theta}\sum_{i=1}^{N-1}\mathbb{E}\big[(Z_{i+1}^{N}(t)-Z_{i}^{N}(t))^{-2\theta}\big]\leq C_{\theta}\,\varepsilon^{2\theta}t^{-\theta}.\end{split} $$

Let $[t_{1},t_{2}]\subset(0,T)$ satisfy $f(t,x)=0$ , $t\notin[t_{1},t_{2}]$ and note that $|\partial_{t}(f-f\phi_{\varepsilon})|\leq C_{f}\,\mathbf{1}_{\{\mathrm{dist}(x^{N},\partial\mathcal{W}_{N})\leq 2\varepsilon\}}$ . Therefore, it holds

$$ \bigg|\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathcal{K}}\partial_{t}(f-f\phi_{\varepsilon})\,\mathrm{d}\nu_{t}\,\mathrm{d}t\bigg|\leq C_{f}\int_{t_{1}}^{t_{2}}\mu_{t}\big(\{x^{N}\in\mathcal{W}_{N}:\,\mathrm{dist}(x^{N},\partial\mathcal{W}_{N})\leq 2\varepsilon\}\big)\,\mathrm{d}t\leq C_{f,\theta}\,\varepsilon^{2\theta}. $$

Arguing similarly, we find that

$$ \bigg|\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathcal{K}}\sum_{1\leq i\leq k\leq N-1}\partial_{x_{i}^{k}x_{i}^{k}}(f-f\phi_{\varepsilon})\,\mathrm{d}\nu_{t}\,\mathrm{d}t\bigg|\leq C_{f,\theta}\,\varepsilon^{2\theta-2}. $$

In addition, Lemma 2.2 and the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality yield

$$ \begin{split}&\,\bigg|\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathcal{K}}\sum_{1\leq i\leq k\leq N}b_{i}^{k}\,\partial_{x_{i}^{k}}(f-f\phi_{\varepsilon})\,\mathrm{d}\nu_{t}\,\mathrm{d}t\bigg|\\
&\leq C_{f}\,\varepsilon^{-1}\sum_{1\leq i\leq k\leq N}\,\int_{t_{1}}^{t_{2}}\int_{\mathcal{K}}|b_{i}^{k}|\,\mathbf{1}_{\{\mathrm{dist}(x^{N},\partial\mathcal{W}_{N})\leq 2\varepsilon\}}\,\mathrm{d}\nu_{t}\,\mathrm{d}t\\
&\leq C_{f,\theta}\,\varepsilon^{-1}\sum_{1\leq i\leq k\leq N}\,\int_{t_{1}}^{t_{2}}\int_{\mathcal{K}^{k}}\bigg(\frac{1}{x_{i}^{k}-x_{i-1}^{k}}+\frac{1}{x_{i+1}^{k}-x_{i}^{k}}\bigg)\,\mathbf{1}_{\{\mathrm{dist}(x^{N},\partial\mathcal{W}_{N})\leq 2\varepsilon\}}\,\prod_{m=k+1}^{N}\lambda^{m,\theta}(x^{m},x^{m-1})\\
&\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\quad\;\mu_{t}(\mathrm{d}x^{N})\,\mathrm{d}x^{k}\,\ldots\,\mathrm{d}x^{N-1}\\
&\leq C_{f.\theta}\,\varepsilon^{-1}\sum_{1\leq i\leq k\leq N}\,\int_{t_{1}}^{t_{2}}\bigg(\int_{\mathcal{K}^{k}}\bigg(\frac{1}{(x_{i}^{k}-x_{i-1}^{k})^{2}}+\frac{1}{(x_{i+1}^{k}-x_{i}^{k})^{2}}\bigg)\prod_{m=k+1}^{N}\lambda^{m,\theta}(x^{m},x^{m-1})\\
&\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\quad\;\mu_{t}(\mathrm{d}x^{N})\,\mathrm{d}x^{k}\,\ldots\,\mathrm{d}x^{N-1}\bigg)^{1/2}\mu_{t}\big(\{x^{N}\in\mathcal{W}_{N}\!:\mathrm{dist}(x^{N},\mathcal{W}_{N})\leq 2\varepsilon\}\big)^{1/2}\,\mathrm{d}t.\end{split} $$

Letting $Z^{k}$ be a $\theta$ -DBM started from $0\in\mathcal{W}_{k}$ , and using Lemma 2.4, Lemma A.1(b), and (3.18), the latter expression can be upper bounded by

$$ C_{f,\theta}\,\varepsilon^{\theta-1}\sum_{1\leq i\leq k\leq N}\,\int_{t_{1}}^{t_{2}}\mathbb{E}\big[(Z_{i}^{k}(t)-Z_{i-1}^{k}(t))^{-2}+(Z_{i+1}^{k}(t)-Z_{i}^{k}(t))^{-2}\big]^{1/2}\,t^{-\theta/2}\,\mathrm{d}t\leq C_{f,\theta}\,\varepsilon^{\theta-1}, $$

where the integral is finite by Lemma A.3(b). It remains to notice that

$$ \begin{split}&\,\bigg|\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathcal{K}}\frac{1}{2}\Delta_{x^{N}}(f-f\phi_{\varepsilon})\,\mathrm{d}\nu_{t}\,\mathrm{d}t\bigg|\\
&\leq C_{f}\int_{t_{1}}^{t_{2}}\int_{\mathcal{W}_{N}}1-\phi_{\varepsilon}\,\mathrm{d}\mu_{t}\,\mathrm{d}t+C_{f}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\,\int_{t_{1}}^{t_{2}}\int_{\mathcal{W}_{N}}|\partial_{x_{i}^{N}}\phi_{\varepsilon}|\,\mathrm{d}\mu_{t}\,\mathrm{d}t+C_{f}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\,\int_{t_{1}}^{t_{2}}\int_{\mathcal{W}_{N}}|\partial_{x_{i}^{N}x_{i}^{N}}\phi_{\varepsilon}|\,\mathrm{d}\mu_{t}\,\mathrm{d}t.\end{split} $$

As before, the three summands can be bounded by $C_{f,\theta}\varepsilon^{2\theta}$ , $C_{f,\theta}\varepsilon^{2\theta-1}$ , and $C_{f,\theta}\varepsilon^{2\theta-2}$ , respectively. Combining the four obtained estimates we arrive at the lemma. ∎

For any $f\in\mathcal{A}_{c}$ , we can now rely on Lemma 3.4 when taking the limit $\varepsilon\downarrow 0$ in

$$ \int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathcal{K}}(\partial_{t}+\mathcal{L}_{1,...,N})(\phi_{\varepsilon}f)\,\mathrm{d}\nu_{t}\,\mathrm{d}t=0 $$

and conclude that

$$ \int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathcal{K}}(\partial_{t}+\mathcal{L}_{1,...,N})f\,\mathrm{d}\nu_{t}\,\mathrm{d}t=0. $$

Step 6. In this final step, we remove the extra assumption on $\mu_{0}$ imposed at the beginning of Step 2.

#### Lemma 3.5.

Fix an $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$ . Then, for any $1\leq p<\theta$ , there exists a constant $C_{\varepsilon,p}<\infty$ such that for all $x^{N}\in\mathcal{W}_{N}$ with $\mathrm{dist}(x^{N},\partial\mathcal{W}_{N})\geq\varepsilon$ and all $1\leq i\leq k\leq N-1$ ,

$$ \int_{\mathcal{K}(x^{N})}\!(x_{i}^{k}-x_{i}^{k+1})^{-p}\,\Lambda^{N,\theta}(x^{N},\mathrm{d}x^{1},\ldots,\mathrm{d}x^{N-1})\,\vee\,\int_{\mathcal{K}(x^{N})}\!(x_{i+1}^{k+1}-x_{i}^{k})^{-p}\,\Lambda^{N,\theta}(x^{N},\mathrm{d}x^{1},\ldots,\mathrm{d}x^{N-1})\leq C_{\varepsilon,p}. $$

Moreover, with $\mathcal{K}_{\delta}(x^{N}):=\{(x_{i}^{k})_{1\leq i\leq k\leq N-1}:\,x_{i}^{k+1}+2\delta\leq x_{i}^{k}+\delta\leq x_{i+1}^{k+1},\,1\leq i\leq k\leq N-1\}$ and $L_{x^{N}}(\mathrm{d}x^{1},\ldots,\mathrm{d}x^{N-1}):=\Lambda^{N,\theta}(x^{N},\mathrm{d}x^{1},\ldots,\mathrm{d}x^{N-1})$ , there exists a constant $C_{\varepsilon}<\infty$ such that for all $x^{N}\in\mathcal{W}_{N}$ with $\mathrm{dist}(x^{N},\partial\mathcal{W}_{N})\geq\varepsilon$ ,

$$ L_{x^{N}}(\mathcal{K}(x^{N})\setminus\mathcal{K}_{\delta}(x^{N}))\leq C_{\varepsilon}\delta. $$

Proof of Lemma 3.5. We just prove the first claim, as the second claim then follows via Markov’s inequality and a union bound. For the first claim, we proceed by backward induction over $k$ . For $k=N-1$ , Lemma 2.2 implies that

$$ \int_{\mathcal{K}^{N-1}(x^{N})}(x_{i}^{N-1}-x_{i}^{N})^{-p}\,\lambda^{N,\theta}(x^{N},x^{N-1})\,\mathrm{d}x^{N-1}\leq C_{p}(x_{i+1}^{N}-x_{i}^{N})^{-p}\leq C_{p}\varepsilon^{-p}=:C_{\varepsilon,p}. $$

For $k<N-1$ , Lemma 2.2 and $(x^{1},\ldots,x^{N-1})\in\mathcal{K}(x^{N})$ give

$$ \begin{split}&\,\int_{\mathcal{K}(x^{N})}(x_{i}^{k}-x_{i}^{k+1})^{-p}\,\Lambda^{N,\theta}(x^{N},\mathrm{d}x^{1},\ldots,\mathrm{d}x^{N-1})\\
&\leq C_{p}\,\int_{\mathcal{K}^{k+1}(x^{N})}(x_{i+1}^{k+1}-x_{i}^{k+1})^{-p}\prod_{m=k+2}^{N}\lambda^{m,\theta}(x^{m},x^{m-1})\,\mathrm{d}x^{k+1}\,\ldots\,\mathrm{d}x^{N}\\
&\leq C_{p}\,\int_{\mathcal{K}^{k+1}(x^{N})}(x_{i+1}^{k+2}-x_{i}^{k+1})^{-p}\prod_{m=k+2}^{N}\lambda^{m,\theta}(x^{m},x^{m-1})\,\mathrm{d}x^{k+1}\,\ldots\,\mathrm{d}x^{N}\leq C_{\varepsilon,p},\end{split} $$

where, in the last line, we have used the induction hypothesis. The first claim readily follows. ∎

To remove the extra assumption on $\mu_{0}$ , we aim to approximate $\mu_{0}$ by $\mu^{n}_{0}$ , $n\in{\mathbb{N}}$ satisfying the extra assumption. Writing $(\mu^{n}_{t})_{t\in[0,T]}$ and $(\nu^{n}_{t})_{t\in[0,T]}$ for the associated flows of probability measures, we then need to check that

$$ \int_{0}^{T}\!\int_{\mathcal{K}}(\partial_{t}+\mathcal{L}_{1,...,N})f\,\mathrm{d}(\nu^{n}_{t}-\nu_{t})\,\mathrm{d}t=\int_{0}^{T}\!\int_{\mathcal{W}_{N}}\!\int_{\mathcal{K}(x^{N})}(\partial_{t}+\mathcal{L}_{1,...,N})f\,\Lambda^{N,\theta}(x^{N},\mathrm{d}x^{1},\ldots,\mathrm{d}x^{N-1})\,\mathrm{d}(\mu^{n}_{t}-\mu_{t})\,\mathrm{d}t $$

goes to $0$ as $n\to\infty$ . Hereby, due to Lemma 3.4, we may assume that for some $\varepsilon>0$ , $f(t,x)=0$ if $\mathrm{dist}(x^{N},\partial\mathcal{W}_{N})<\varepsilon$ . Our first claim is that

$$ h(t,x^{N}):=\int_{\mathcal{K}(x^{N})}(\partial_{t}+\mathcal{L}_{1,...,N})f\,\Lambda^{N,\theta}(x^{N},\mathrm{d}x^{1},\ldots,\mathrm{d}x^{N-1}) $$

is continuous in $x^{N}\!\in\!\mathcal{W}_{N}$ . If $\mathrm{dist}(x^{N},\partial\mathcal{W}_{N})<\varepsilon$ , we have $h\equiv 0$ in a neighborhood of $x^{N}$ .

Now, consider $x^{N}\in\mathcal{W}_{N}$ such that $\mathrm{dist}(x^{N},\partial\mathcal{W}_{N})\geq\varepsilon$ and let $x^{N,n}\rightarrow x^{N}$ with $\mathrm{dist}(x^{N,n},x^{N})<\varepsilon/2$ for all $n$ . For $\delta\in(0,\varepsilon/4)$ , we bound the derivatives of $f$ by a constant and use Lemma 3.5 to obtain

$$ \begin{split}&\,\bigg|\int_{\mathcal{K}(x^{N,n})\setminus\mathcal{K}_{\delta}(x^{N,n})}\Big(\partial_{t}f+\frac{1}{2}\Delta_{x}f\Big)(t,x^{N,n},x^{1},\ldots,x^{N-1})\,\Lambda^{N,\theta}(x^{N,n},\mathrm{d}x^{1},\ldots,\mathrm{d}x^{N-1})\bigg|\\
&\leq C_{f}L_{x^{N,n}}(\mathcal{K}(x^{N,n})\setminus\mathcal{K}_{\delta}(x^{N,n}))\leq C_{f,\frac{\varepsilon}{2}}\,\delta.\end{split} $$

For the same reason,

$$ \bigg|\int_{\mathcal{K}(x^{N})\setminus\mathcal{K}_{\delta}(x^{N})}\Big(\partial_{t}f+\frac{1}{2}\Delta_{x}f\Big)(t,x)\,\Lambda^{N,\theta}(x^{N},\mathrm{d}x^{1},\ldots,\mathrm{d}x^{N-1})\bigg|\leq C_{f,\varepsilon}\delta. $$

Moreover, by the Bounded Convergence Theorem,

$$ \begin{split}&\lim_{n\to\infty}\,\int_{\mathbb{R}^{\frac{(N-1)N}{2}}}\mathbf{1}_{\mathcal{K}(x^{N,n})\cap\mathcal{K}_{\delta}(x^{N,n})}\,\Big(\partial_{t}f+\frac{1}{2}\Delta_{x}f\Big)(t,x^{N,n},x^{1},\ldots,x^{N-1})\,\Lambda^{N,\theta}(x^{N,n},x^{1},\ldots,x^{N-1})\\
&\qquad\qquad\qquad\;-\mathbf{1}_{\mathcal{K}(x^{N})\cap\mathcal{K}_{\delta}(x^{N})}\Big(\partial_{t}f+\frac{1}{2}\Delta_{x}f\Big)(t,x)\,\Lambda^{N,\theta}(x^{N},x^{1},\ldots,x^{N-1})\,\mathrm{d}x^{1}\,\ldots\,\mathrm{d}x^{N-1}=0.\end{split} $$

Therefore, $\int_{\mathcal{K}(x^{N})}\big(\partial_{t}f+\frac{1}{2}\Delta_{x}f\big)(t,x)\,\Lambda^{N,\theta}(x^{N},\mathrm{d}x^{1},\ldots,\mathrm{d}x^{N-1})$ is continuous at $x^{N}$ .

Fix $p\in(1,\theta)$ , and let $q$ satisfy $p^{-1}+q^{-1}=1$ . Then, bounding $\partial_{x_{i}^{k}}f$ by a constant and employing Hölder’s inequality we have, with the convention $x^{k,n}=x^{k}$ for $k=1,\,2,\,\ldots,\,N-1$ ,

$$ \begin{split}&\,\bigg|\int_{\mathcal{K}(x^{N,n})\setminus\mathcal{K}_{\delta}(x^{N,n})}b_{i}^{k}(x^{k,n},x^{k-1})\,\partial_{x_{i}^{k}}f(t,x^{N,n},x^{1},\ldots,x^{N-1})\,\Lambda^{N,\theta}(x^{N,n},\mathrm{d}x^{1},\ldots,\mathrm{d}x^{N-1})\bigg|\\
&\leq C_{f}\bigg(\int_{\mathbb{R}^{\frac{(N-1)N}{2}}}\mathbf{1}_{\mathcal{K}(x^{N,n})\setminus\mathcal{K}_{\delta}(x^{N,n})}\,\Lambda^{N,\theta}(x^{N,n},\mathrm{d}x^{1},\ldots,\mathrm{d}x^{N-1})\bigg)^{1/q}\\
&\quad\cdot\bigg(\int_{\mathbb{R}^{\frac{(N-1)N}{2}}}\big((x_{i}^{k-1}-x_{i}^{k,n})^{-p}+(x_{i}^{k,n}-x_{i-1}^{k-1})^{-p}\big)\,\Lambda^{N,\theta}(x^{N,n},\mathrm{d}x^{1},\ldots,\mathrm{d}x^{N-1})\bigg)^{1/p}\leq C_{f,\frac{\varepsilon}{2},p}\,\delta^{1/q},\end{split} $$

where the last inequality is due to Lemmas 3.5 and 2.2. The same argument also shows that

$$ \bigg|\int_{\mathcal{K}(x^{N})\setminus\mathcal{K}_{\delta}(x^{N})}b_{i}^{k}(x^{k},x^{k-1})\,\partial_{x_{i}^{k}}f(t,x)\,\Lambda^{N,\theta}(x^{N},\mathrm{d}x^{1},\ldots,\mathrm{d}x^{N-1})\bigg|\leq C_{f,\varepsilon,p}\,\delta^{1/q}. $$

Consequently,

$$ \begin{split}&\bigg|\int_{\mathcal{K}(x^{N,n})}b_{i}^{k}(x^{k,n},x^{k-1})\,\partial_{x_{i}^{k}}f(t,x^{N,n},x^{1},\ldots,x^{N-1})\,\Lambda^{N,\theta}(x^{N,n},\mathrm{d}x^{1},\ldots,\mathrm{d}x^{N-1})\\
&\,-\int_{\mathcal{K}(x^{N})}b_{i}^{k}(x^{k},x^{k-1})\,\partial_{x_{i}^{k}}f(t,x)\,\Lambda^{N,\theta}(x^{N},\mathrm{d}x^{1},\ldots,\mathrm{d}x^{N-1})\bigg|\\
&\leq C_{f,\frac{\varepsilon}{2},p}\,\delta^{1/q}+C_{f,\varepsilon,p}\,\delta^{1/q}\\
&\quad+\int_{\mathbb{R}^{\frac{(N-1)N}{2}}}\Big|\mathbf{1}_{\mathcal{K}(x^{N,n})\cap\mathcal{K}_{\delta}(x^{N,n})}\,b_{i}^{k}(x^{k,n},x^{k-1})\,\partial_{x_{i}^{k}}f(t,x^{N,n},x^{1},\ldots,x^{N-1})\,\Lambda^{N,\theta}(x^{N,n},x^{1},\ldots,x^{N-1})\\
&\qquad\qquad\qquad\;-\mathbf{1}_{\mathcal{K}(x^{N})\cap\mathcal{K}_{\delta}(x^{N})}\,b_{i}^{k}(x^{k},x^{k-1})\,\partial_{x_{i}^{k}}f(t,x)\,\Lambda^{N,\theta}(x^{N},x^{1},\ldots,x^{N-1})\Big|\,\mathrm{d}x^{1}\,\ldots\,\mathrm{d}x^{N-1}.\end{split} $$

The last integral goes to $0$ as $n\to\infty$ by the Bounded Convergence Theorem. Taking $n\to\infty$ and then $\delta\downarrow 0$ , we see that $h(t,x^{N})$ is continuous in $x^{N}\in\mathcal{W}_{N}$ . Since $h$ is bounded (recall $f\in\mathcal{A}_{c}$ and (3.20)),

$$ \int_{\mathcal{K}}(\partial_{t}+\mathcal{L}_{1,...,N})f\,\mathrm{d}(\nu^{n}_{t}-\nu_{t})=\int_{\mathcal{W}_{N}}\int_{\mathcal{K}(x^{N})}(\partial_{t}+\mathcal{L}_{1,...,N})f\,\Lambda^{N,\theta}(x^{N},\mathrm{d}x^{1},\ldots,\mathrm{d}x^{N-1})\,\mathrm{d}(\mu^{n}_{t}-\mu_{t}) $$

goes to $0$ in the limit $n\to\infty$ , as long as the weak convergence $\mu^{n}_{t}\to\mu_{t}$ holds.

Next, we observe that thanks to estimate (3.5) and Lemma A.1(b),

$$ \begin{split}\int_{\mathcal{W}_{N}}\int_{\mathcal{K}(x^{N})}(\partial_{t}+\mathcal{L}_{1,...,N})f\,\Lambda^{N,\theta}(x^{N},\mathrm{d}x^{1},\ldots,\mathrm{d}x^{N-1})\,\mathrm{d}\mu_{t}&\leq C+C\sum_{k=2}^{N}\sum_{i=1}^{k-1}\mathbb{E}\bigg[\frac{1}{X_{i+1}^{k}(t)-X_{i}^{k}(t)}\bigg]\\
&\leq C+C\sum_{k=2}^{N}\sum_{i=1}^{k-1}\mathbb{E}\bigg[\frac{1}{Z_{i+1}^{k}(t)-Z_{i}^{k}(t)}\bigg],\end{split} $$

where each $X^{k}$ is a $\theta$ -DBM with initial density $\int_{\mathcal{K}^{k+1}}\!\prod_{m=k+1}^{N}\!\lambda^{m,\theta}(x^{m},x^{m-1})\,\mathrm{d}x^{k+1}\ldots\mathrm{d}x^{N-1}\mu_{0}(\mathrm{d}x^{N})$ and each $Z^{k}$ is a $\theta$ -DBM started from $0\in\mathcal{W}_{k}$ . The latter upper bound is integrable over $[0,T]$ thanks to Lemma A.3(b), so that by the Dominated Covergence Theorem, the quantities in (3.19) go to $0$ in the limit $n\to\infty$ , as long as the weak convergence $\mu^{n}_{t}\to\mu_{t}$ holds for all $t\in[0,T]$ .

In view of Lemma A.2, the Fokker-Planck equation (3.3) is fulfilled for every probability measure $\mu_{0}$ on $\mathcal{W}_{N}$ such that $\mu_{0}$ can be approximated in the $1$ -Wasserstein distance by probability measures $\mu_{0}^{n}$ on $\mathcal{W}_{N}$ for which (3.3) has been established. If $\mu_{0}$ is a Dirac mass at $x\in\,\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\circ}}{{\mathcal{W}}}_{N}$ , a desired approximation is given by the convolutions with a scaled bump function, which satisfy the extra assumption imposed at the beginning of Step 2. If $\mu_{0}$ is a Dirac mass at $x\in\partial{\mathcal{W}_{N}}$ , a desired approximation is given by the Dirac masses at $\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\circ}}{{\mathcal{W}}}_{N}\,\ni x^{n}$ , $x^{n}_{i}:=x_{i}+\frac{i}{n}$ . Thus, (3.3) holds for any $\mu_{0}$ given by a finite convex combination of Dirac masses in $\mathcal{W}_{N}$ . Since every probability measure $\mu_{0}$ on $\mathcal{W}_{N}$ can be approximated in the $1$ -Wasserstein distance by such convex combinations, the proof of (3.3) is finished. ∎

## 4. Proof of Theorem 1.1

Section 3.2 allows us to apply Proposition 3.3, hence concluding the existence of a solution $\eta$ to the martingale problem associated with $\mathcal{L}_{1,...,N}$ such that $\eta\circ e_{t}^{-1}=\nu_{t}$ , $t\in[0,T]$ . A standard localization argument shows that $\eta$ is a solution to the local martingale problem in the sense of [18, Chapter 5, Definition 4.5]. By [18, Chapter 5, Proposition 4.6], $\eta$ induces a weak solution to the SDE (1.5). The remaining statements of Theorem 1.1 are restated for convenience in the next proposition.

#### Proposition 4.1.

Let $\eta$ be a solution to the martingale problem associated with $\mathcal{L}_{1,...,N}$ such that $\eta\circ e_{t}^{-1}=\nu_{t}$ , $t\geq 0$ , and let $X=(X_{i}^{k})_{1\leq i\leq k\leq N}$ be distributed according to $\eta$ . Then:

- (a) $X$ is a Markov process.

- (b) If $\eta^{\prime}$ also satisfies the assumptions of the proposition, then $\eta^{\prime}=\eta$ .

- (c) Each $X^{k}$ is a $\theta$ -DBM.

Proof. (a). The proof closely follows [18, Chapter 5, Lemma 4.19 and Theorem 4.20], so we omit the details that are the same and emphasize the differences. Fix a $t_{0}>0$ , and for $\omega\in C\big([0,t_{0}],\mathbb{R}^{\frac{N(N+1)}{2}}\big)$ , let $Q_{\omega}$ be the regular conditional distribution $\eta$ given $\mathcal{G}_{t_{0}}:=\sigma(s\mapsto\omega(s),\,s\in[0,t_{0}])$ . Write $\theta_{t_{0}}$ for the time shift operator, and define $P_{\omega}=Q_{\omega}\circ\theta_{t_{0}}^{-1}$ . For given $0\!\leq\!s\!<\!t\!<\!\infty$ and $f\in C_{b}^{2}\big(\mathbb{R}^{\frac{N(N+1)}{2}}\big)$ , set
